We give the weighted cohomology calculation explicitly; simply
replacing $1$ by $kl$ in an acyclicity assertion would be incorrect.
The two quotient charts $x\ne0$, $y\ne0$ are finite quotients
of affine lines, and their overlap is a finite quotient of a
punctured line.  Finite averaging and Stein acyclicity compute
coherent cohomology by this two-chart complex.  Its homogeneous
Laurent monomials give
\[
 \begin{split}
 h^0\mathcal O(a)&=\#\{(i,j)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2:mi+nj=a\},\\
 h^1\mathcal O(a)&=h^0\mathcal O(-a-d).
 \end{split}
\]
The second equality identifies the remaining monomials
$x^{-i-1}y^{-j-1}$; it does not require a positivity theorem.
The bundles $\mathcal O(-z),\mathcal O(-2z)$ are acyclic.
Indeed a possible degree-one monomial would give
$m(i+1)+n(j+1)=az$, with $a=1$ or $2$.
Coprimality forces $i+1=lA$, $j+1=kB$, hence
$3A+4B=a$ with $A,B\ge1$, which is impossible.
Positive degree has no degree-one monomials, so
$H^1\mathcal O(z)=0$ as used above.

Put $b=d-12z$.  Both $b$ and $b-z$ are negative.
Degree-one monomials for $\mathcal O(b)$ would satisfy
$3A+4B=12$, with $A,B\ge1$, and none exist.
For $\mathcal O(b-z)$ the equation is $3A+4B=13$;
its only positive solution is $(A,B)=(3,1)$, producing
$x^{3l-2}y^{k-2}$ in the dual description.  It is allowed
exactly when $k>1$; write $e_k=1$ in that case and $e_k=0$
otherwise.  Projection formula and the two-column Leray sequence
now give
\[
 h^\bullet(\mathcal V)=(1,1,0,0),\qquad
 h^\bullet(\mathcal H)=(0,0,e_k,e_k),\qquad
 h^\bullet(\mathcal T)=(1,1,e_k,e_k).
\]
The program \texttt{e\_push\_exact.py} independently checks these
counts for all $1965$ coprime pairs with $k,l\le80$; the monomial
argument proves them for all pairs.

On the normalization $\nu:E=\mathrm{dP}_6\to W\subset X$,
the branchwise normal line is $K_E$: the invariant cusp form
$d\log x_1\wedge d\log x_2\wedge dq$ trivializes $K_X$
on the entire cusp neighbourhood.  Local normal coefficients
therefore give the exact sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal T\longrightarrow T_X
 \longrightarrow\nu_*K_E\longrightarrow0,
 \qquad h^\bullet(K_E)=(0,0,1).
\]
We must determine its connecting map when $k>1$.
The dual logarithmic sequence, tensored with $K_X$, has horizontal
subline $\bar f^*\mathcal O(13z-2d)$ and vertical quotient
$\bar f^*(\mathcal O(z-d)\oplus\mathcal O(2z-d))$.
The latter has no global sections, by the same equations
$3A+4B=1,2$ above.  Consequently
\[
 H^0(\Omega_X^1(\log W)\otimes K_X)
 =H^0(\mathfrak B,\mathcal O(13z-2d)).
\]
For $k>1$ this is generated by the monomial
$x^{3l-2}y^{k-2}$ multiplying the horizontal logarithmic
differential.  Both $x$ and $y$ are nonzero over $p_0$, so its
residue on $E$ is nonzero.  The ordinary logarithmic residue
sequence, tensored with $K_X$, identifies this residue map with
the Serre dual of
$H^2(E,K_E)\to H^3(X,\mathcal T)$.
One can check this identification directly in each chart
$q=z_0z_1z_2$: the residues of $dq/q$ are one on each branch,
and contraction with the invariant three-form is the normal
coefficient pairing.  Thus that connecting map has rank $e_k$.
The long exact sequence proves $h^2(T_X)=1$ and $h^3(T_X)=0$;
degrees zero and one are unchanged.

Finally $\partial_c\Pi=e\otimes\gamma$ gives the constant
groupoid cocycle $\lambda\mapsto\gamma(\lambda)e$ on every
regular torus.  On the enlarged finite roots the derivative of the
affine generator is $(r_j/m_j)e$, and the derivative of its
punctured connector is $(\log s_j)/(2\pi i)\,r_je$.
The identity $m_j(r_j/m_j)=\gamma(w_j)$ verifies the power
relation, while $\gamma A_j=\gamma$ verifies conjugation with
every lattice arrow.  Changing $\log s_j$ by $2\pi i N$
adds the derivative of the integral arrow $Nw_j$; the connector
formula is used only on the punctured overlap.  Its central
root-chart representative is the constant $(r_j/m_j)e$,
which is holomorphic.  At the cusp $\gamma$ kills the toric periods,
so the constant deck cocycle is exactly its extending cocycle
above.  Its image under the two isomorphisms
$H^1(\mathcal V)\simeq H^1(\mathcal T)\simeq H^1(T_X)$
is $e\otimes[\gamma]\ne0$.  The chain rule gives the asserted
$u$-class.  The Kuranishi local algebra is
$\mathbb C\{t\}/I$ since $h^1=1$.  The existing family induces
$t\mapsto g(c)$ with $g'(c_0)\ne0$.  The analytic inverse
function theorem makes this substitution injective; every
element of $I$ maps to zero, so $I=0$.  Its classifying map is
then an isomorphism of germs, proving local miniversality.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[local separation and canonical dimension]\label{push:src:E.2.2}
The multiplicity pair $(3k,4l)$ is constant on every sufficiently
small deformation of one of the preceding members.  Distinct
pairs therefore determine disjoint open loci among these
isomorphism classes.  Moreover
\[
 \kappa(X)=\begin{cases}-\infty,&kl<3k+4l,\\1,&kl>3k+4l.
 \end{cases}
\]
Equality $kl=3k+4l$ never occurs under $\gcd(3k,4l)=1$.
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{push:src:E.1.2}; \cref{push:src:E.2.1}}

\begin{proof}
Local miniversality identifies every small deformation with the
fixed-data period family; \ref{push:src:E.1.2} makes its multiplicity pair an
intrinsic biholomorphic invariant.  The canonical formula of
\ref{push:src:E.2.1} and connected fibres identify its pluricanonical sections
with those of $\mathcal O(r(kl-3k-4l))$ on the root curve.
Negative weight has no sections.  Positive weight has linearly
growing section counts along multiples of $12kl$, giving
Kodaira dimension one.  Equality would imply $k\mid4l$;
coprimality forces $k=1$, and then $l=3+4l$ is impossible.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[separation in irreducible analytic families]\label{push:src:E.2.3}
Suppose a proper holomorphic submersion over a connected
irreducible reduced complex base has two fibres of the type
in \ref{push:src:E.2.1}.  Then their multiplicity pairs agree, even if some
other fibres have not been constructed by this method.
For these members the asymptotic number
\[
 s(X)=\lim_{r\to\infty}
 \frac{h^0(X,K_X^r)-h^0(X,K_X^{-r})}{r}
 =\frac1{12}-\frac1{3k}-\frac1{4l}
\]
recovers the ordered multiplicity pair uniquely.
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{push:src:E.2.1}; \cite[Chapter III, Theorem 4.1]{BS76}}

\begin{proof}
For coprime $m,n$, the number of nonnegative solutions of
$mi+nj=N$ is $N/(mn)+O(1)$ as $N\to\infty$:
there is one permitted residue class of $j$ modulo $m$, and
its representatives lie between $0$ and $N/n$.
The canonical formula in \ref{push:src:E.2.1} proves the displayed limit,
with a negative value when the anticanonical counts grow.
Write $1/12-s(X)=a/b$ in lowest positive terms.
Since $\gcd(m+n,mn)=1$, we have $a=m+n$, $b=mn$.
Thus $m,n$ are the two roots of $T^2-aT+b$.
Their order is determined because only $m$ is divisible by
three and only $n$ is divisible by four.

For every fixed integer $r$, apply the finite-free-complex
theorem of \cite[Chapter III, Theorem 4.1]{BS76} to
the relative canonical power, which is an invertible flat
sheaf for a holomorphic submersion.  Its zeroth cohomology
dimension has analytic jumping loci.  On an irreducible
base any value constant on a nonempty open set is its
generic value: a proper analytic jumping locus has empty
interior.  Local miniversality in \ref{push:src:E.2.1} makes these dimensions
constant near either of the two given fibres, since all
nearby fibres have the same multiplicities and their
canonical formula is independent of the period parameter.
Consequently the two fibres have equal dimensions for
every positive and negative $r$.  Their limits $s(X)$
are equal, and the preceding arithmetic recovers the same
pair.  This proof uses relative cohomology only; it makes
no general invariance assertion for Kodaira dimension.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Analytic foundations and the version 1}\label{push:section:E.3}
\begin{proposition}[base change and duality]\label{push:src:E.3.1}
For the proper flat root-curve morphisms in \ref{push:src:E.2.1}, the canonical
geometric-point comparison
\[
 (R^q\bar f_*\mathcal O_X)\otimes k(b)
 \longrightarrow H^q(X_b,\mathcal O_{X_b})
\]
is an isomorphism for $q=0,1,2$, and the direct images are locally
free.  The trace induces the canonical isomorphism
\[
 (R^2\bar f_*\mathcal O_X)^\vee
 \simeq\bar f_*\omega_{X/\mathfrak B}.
\]
Both comparisons descend on the analytic root-curve groupoid.
These conclusions, and hence the use made of them in \cref{fam:src:A.5.2}, require
no result specific to the version 1 of
\cite{DuEtAl2026v1}.
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{push:src:E.2.1}; \cref{fam:src:A.5.2}; \cite{DuEtAl2026v1}; \cref{app:rederive:push-src-E.3.1}; \cite[Section 6, Hauptsatz I, and Section 7, Satz 5]{Grauert1960D}; \cite{Grauert1963ErratumD}; \cite[Chapter III, Theorem 4.1]{BS76}}


This is analytic base change and duality, with the source hypotheses specified in the re-derivation. A complete re-derivation is given in Appendix~\ref{app:rederive:push-src-E.3.1}.


Grauert's original direct-image theorem
\cite[Section 6, Hauptsatz I, and Section 7, Satz 5]{Grauert1960D}
was also opened together with its correction \cite{Grauert1963ErratumD}.
The correction explicitly warns that the exceptional locus in
Section 7, Satz 2 need not be closed.  \ref{push:src:E.3.1} uses the
constant-cohomology theorem on every chart and the later
base-change formulation, so it does not make that erroneous
closedness inference.  For a generic argument over a smooth
curve one can instead use the finite free complex of
\cite[Chapter III, Theorem 4.1]{BS76}; its rank-jump minors
give the required local analytic exceptional sets.

\begin{proposition}[the five historical claims]\label{push:src:E.3.2}
For the standard twist vectors, each of the five named theorems
in the attached version 1 of \cite{DuEtAl2026v1} has a complete
argument relative to the explicitly constructed family and the
standard analytic theorems it cites.  We located no failed step
in those five arguments.  Their assertions are not present in
the attached version 2 \cite{DuEtAl2026v2}.  This textual
difference carries no inference about their mathematical truth
or about the reason for their omission.
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cite{DuEtAl2026v1}; \cite{DuEtAl2026v2}; \cref{push:src:E.3.1}; \cite[Theorem 7.4]{PY16push}; \cref{push:src:E.2.1}; \cref{fam:src:B.4.1}}

\begin{proof}
We give the dependency audit, rather than infer correctness from
the occurrence of the theorem labels.

For \texttt{p2:thm:tangent-cohomology}, the proof first constructs
the root lift as an actual Cartesian quotient, proves properness
and flatness on its atlas, and computes the cusp normalization
resolution with the multiplicative cup pairing.  The two lemmas
\texttt{p2:lem:analytic-grauert} and
\texttt{p2:lem:analytic-relative-duality} explicitly cite the
standard results checked in \ref{push:src:E.3.1} and perform descent; they do
not assume an unproved general stack duality principle.  Its
weighted cohomology and the normal sequence then give
$(1,1,1,0)$.  Its algebraic-to-analytic Picard comparison invokes
the applicable proper-stack GAGA theorem
\cite[Theorem 7.4]{PY16push}; the direct analytic Picard
argument in \ref{push:src:E.2.1} provides another justification.  Our general
calculation reduces to precisely its four acyclic weights
$-1,-2,-5,-6$ at $k=l=1$.  The extra logarithmic cohomology
for $k>1$ is outside that source's assertion.

For \texttt{p2:thm:kuranishi-aut}, the generating-arrow formulas
are $\gamma(\lambda)e$ on a lattice arrow, $0$ on a core deck
arrow, $e/3,-e/4$ on the two affine root generators, and
$\gamma(\lambda)e$ on a cusp arrow.  Its proof verifies the
relations, uses logarithms only on punctured connectors, and
uses the extending toric logarithmic vector on the cusp.
The Leray edge isomorphism carries this class to
$e\otimes[\gamma]\ne0$.  Completeness of the Kuranishi family
then gives a substitution $t\mapsto g(s)$ with $g'(0)\ne0$;
injectivity forces the entire defining ideal, including any
nilpotents, to vanish.  This proves a smooth reduced germ and
miniversality, without incorrectly claiming uniqueness or
universality.  The same theorem proves only
$\operatorname{Aut}^0=\mathbb C^*$: its flow has kernel
$\mathbb Z$, verified on the normalization of the cusp.  Full
automorphisms are treated separately below.

For \texttt{p2:thm:intrinsic-fibration}, adjunction and the
local finite characters give $K^{-2}=f^*\mathcal O_B(1)$.
Connected fibres and the projection formula identify all its
sections with the two base sections.  The complete pencil
therefore forces a biholomorphism to cover a base automorphism.
The three different multiplicity and monodromy types distinguish
the marked values, so this base automorphism is the identity.
This is the same argument as A.1 of the original return; it
needs no assertion that an arbitrary biholomorphism was
initially fibre preserving.

For \texttt{p2:thm:exact-period}, the simultaneous centralizer
is computed entrywise, and the period columns force integral
parameter difference.  Normalization after the genuine cyclic
base change tests the actual affine deck action, giving the
order-four parity obstruction.  Sufficiency is explicit:
choose $F^3=t$, $G^4=t-1$ and
$\ell=(2\pi i)^{-1}\log(F/G)$ on the universal cover, modulo
integral constants.  The source's translation is
\[
 b_{a,h}=-\frac h{12}\Pi_a\widehat\gamma+h\ell e.
\]
Its defects at $g_1,g_2,g_0$ are respectively
\[
 \tfrac h2(\widehat u-\widehat w-\widehat\delta),\qquad
 \tfrac h2(-\widehat w+\widehat\delta),\qquad0.
\]
For even $h$ these are integral.  Removing the known logarithmic
connector on each root chart leaves a holomorphic translation;
at the cusp $\ell=-s/12+$ a holomorphic function cancels the
period's logarithm.  Thus both the map and its inverse extend
over all three fillings.  Appendix calculations give the raw
composition defect $-hk\,e/12$ and the correction
$-h^2e/24$, which makes the action strict.  These identities
were re-executed exactly in
\texttt{code/e\_push\_source\_audit.py}.  The return's torsor
argument is another sufficiency proof, not a repair of a
missing proof in this source.

For \texttt{p2:thm:full-automorphisms}, a self-map's linear
part is first forced to be the identity.  The integral middle
translation cohomology is $\mathbb Z$, with representative
$c_N(g_1)=N(0,1,-2,0)^t$, $c_N(g_2)=0$.
The cusp defect is $N(0,-1,1,0)^t$, whose residual class in
$\Lambda/(\mathbb Z\widehat w+\mathbb Z\widehat\delta)$ is
$(0,-N)$.  A transverse disc through a smooth central point
lifts to the free cusp cover, forcing that residual monodromy
to vanish.  Hence $N=0$.  For the remaining zero class the
local quotient lift gives meromorphic character ratios; their
already single-valued additive logarithms have zero winding,
so the ratios are units and their logarithms extend.  Finite
averaging gives extension on both complete root discs.  The
result is a global section of the vertical bundle, hence a
constant multiple of $e$.  Its period kernel is $\mathbb Z$.
This proves $\operatorname{Aut}=\mathbb C^*$, including the
absence of disconnected components.  It corresponds to the
integral-cocycle and cusp-extension steps of \cref{fam:src:B.4.1}.

The audit program records attachment SHA-256 hashes and all five
label locations in version 1; every label and the corresponding
Kuranishi, Kodaira--Spencer, parity-classification and tangent
statements are absent from version 2.  We separately opened the
version-specific arXiv records and treat these as preprint
versions, not as a journal publication verified by its title.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[limits of the overlap]\label{push:src:E.3.3}
The five audited version-1 results concern the standard
$(3,4)$ twist data.  That text does not classify general twist
vectors, compute the exact maximum $M$, construct a filling as
the family parameter tends to zero, compute a class in
$\Theta_7$, or settle the boundary questions in Parts A--D.
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{fam:src:C.1.1,fam:src:C.2.3}}

\begin{proof}
Its finite generators use only
$\widehat\gamma+2\widehat u-4\widehat w$ and
$-\widehat\gamma-3\widehat u+3\widehat w$ throughout the
deformation and classification arguments.  The cusp completion
constructed there fills the elliptic-base puncture for a fixed
period parameter; it is not a filling at zero of the parameter
$w$.  Its period domain is an admissible region, without the
maximization or the interval certificate of \cref{fam:src:C.1.1,fam:src:C.2.3}.  The concluding
orbit groupoid, quadratic correction, and the Oka results do not
supply the missing parameter degenerations or their topology.
Thus none of these omitted conclusions can be read into the
five theorems merely from the words ``family'' or ``cusp''.
\end{proof}

\subsection{An independent interval certificate}\label{push:section:E.4}
\label{sec:e4}

We write $\eta_D$ for the Dedekind eta function and set
\[
 h=z-(1-\tau)/2,\qquad
 \mathcal N^2(z,\tau)=
 \left|\frac{\vartheta_3(h,\tau)}{\eta_D(\tau)}\right|^2
 \exp\left(-\frac{2\pi(\Im h)^2}{\Im\tau}\right).
\]
The half-period theta identity identifies this with the norm used in
\cref{fam:src:C.1.1,fam:src:C.2.3}. The coefficient of $\Im c$ in $D_c$ is one. Consequently the
identity from the period calculation above which we use is
\[
 D_{\rm part}=\frac6\pi
 \log\left(\frac{\mathcal N}{2\sqrt3}\right).
\]
It follows directly by taking the imaginary part of the theta formula
for $\beta^{\rm part}$; its Gaussian factor removes
$6(\Im\mu)^2/\Im\tau$. Thus no numerical normalization is inferred
from the new computation. The analytic formula and the first
certificate are recorded in the period calculation above, \cref{fam:src:C.1.1,fam:src:C.2.3}. The result below supplies independent
arithmetic evidence for that same conclusion, with the independent certificate below.

\begin{theorem}[independent certification of every box]\label{push:src:E.4.1}
For all 19701 rational rectangles in the supplied certificate, and for
each $\tau$ in the rectangle, both zeros of $\wp_\tau$ satisfy
$\mathcal N^2<2$. The new largest certified upper bound is less than
\[
 1.999877571767410525.
\]
The 19701 rectangles, 36 local rectangles and 174 excluded rectangles
have disjoint interiors and cover exactly
$[0,1/2]\times[17/20,2]$. Every local rectangle is contained in
$|\tau-i|<3/20000$, and every excluded rectangle satisfies
$|\tau|<1$ throughout.
\end{theorem}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \citet[Sections 2--3]{Johansson2016}; \citet{PythonFlint2026}}


\begin{proof}
The programs \path{code/e4_arb_certificate.py} and
\path{code/e4_cover_and_local.py} use respectively 192-bit and 256-bit
Arb arithmetic through python-flint 0.9.0. The arithmetic implementation
is independent of mpmath. We import neither mpmath nor any routine
from the previous certificate. The only numerical data taken from that
certificate are its rational rectangle endpoints. We recompute roots,
preconditioners, radii, contraction bounds, function values and tails.
Arb's midpoint-radius representation and its outward error bounds are
described by \citet[Sections 2--3]{Johansson2016}; the precise
constructor and endpoint semantics used here are documented in
\citet{PythonFlint2026}. The final comparison is made with an upper
endpoint, before conversion to a decimal string.

For a rectangle $Q$, let $z_0$ and $A\ne0$ be the exact dyadic complex
numbers selected by the midpoint Newton iteration. That iteration is
only a choice of constants. For $Z=z_0+[-r,r]+i[-r,r]$ we independently
enclose $\wp_\tau(z_0)$ and $\wp'_\tau(Z)$ for $\tau\in Q$.
We accept only if
\[
 \begin{split}
 &\left|-A\wp_\tau(z_0)
 +(1-A\wp'_\tau(Z))(Z-z_0)\right|_\infty<r,\\
 &|\Re(1-A\wp'_\tau(Z))|
       +|\Im(1-A\wp'_\tau(Z))|<1.
 \end{split}
\]
Here absolute values on enclosures mean their outward upper bounds.
The derivative enclosure and integration along a line segment show
that $z\mapsto z-A\wp_\tau(z)$ is a strict contraction of $Z$ into
itself, uniformly for $\tau\in Q$. Thus it has a genuine zero in $Z$.
The two zeros of $\wp$ are negatives modulo the period lattice, counted
with multiplicity. The theta transformation laws show that
$\mathcal N$ is invariant under these operations; hence one root
enclosure controls both zeros. No continuity or success of Newton
iteration is used in that conclusion.

We use the normally convergent cosine expansion
\[
 \wp_\tau(z)=\frac{\pi^2}{\sin^2\pi z}-\frac{\pi^2}{3}
 +8\pi^2\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{nq^n}{1-q^n}
                      (1-\cos 2\pi nz),\qquad q=e^{2\pi i\tau},
\]
and differentiate it in $z$ for $\wp'$. This identity follows by twice
differentiating the normally convergent Jacobi product and inserting
$E_2=1-24\sum_{n\geq1}nq^n/(1-q^n)$; this also verifies the
Fourier formula used in the period calculation above. The new program sums
32 terms directly in cosine form. Put $r_q\geq|q|$,
$H_z\geq|\Im z|$, and $R_q=r_q e^{2\pi H_z}<1$.
For $j=1,2$, the inequality $(N+k)^j\leq(N+1)^jk^j$ gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 U_1(a)&=\frac{(N+1)a^{N+1}}{(1-a)^2},\\
 U_2(a)&=\frac{(N+1)^2a^{N+1}(1+a)}{(1-a)^3},
 \qquad
 \sum_{n>N}n^j a^n\leq U_j(a).
 \end{aligned}
\]
We therefore add complex rectangles enclosing discs of radii
\[
 \frac{8\pi^2}{1-r_q}\bigl(U_1(r_q)+U_1(R_q)\bigr),
 \qquad \frac{16\pi^3}{1-r_q}U_2(R_q)
\]
to the two partial sums. These estimates follow from
$|\cos z|,|\sin z|\leq e^{|\Im z|}$ and
$|1-q^n|\geq1-r_q$. They differ from the moment formulas used in
the old implementation.

For $\vartheta_3$ we sum
$1+2\sum_{n=1}^{12}e^{\pi i n^2\tau}\cos(2\pi nh)$.
With $T_*\leq\Im\tau$ and $H_*\geq|\Im h|$, the remaining
absolute value is at most
\[
 \frac{2e^{-169\pi T_*+26\pi H_*}}
 {1-e^{-27\pi T_*+2\pi H_*}}.
\]
The ratio in this expression is tested to be less than one. For eta
we independently sum its logarithm,
\[
 \log\eta_D(\tau)=\frac{\pi i\tau}{12}
          +\sum_{n=1}^{24}\log(1-q^n)+\mathcal E,
 \qquad
 |\mathcal E|\leq
 \frac{r_q^{25}}{(1-r_q)(1-r_q^{25})}.
\]
The logarithms are holomorphic on $|q^n|<1$. The tail follows by
summing $|\log(1-z)|\leq|z|/(1-|z|)$.
We enclose $\mathcal N^2$ as
\[
 ((\Re\vartheta_3)^2+(\Im\vartheta_3)^2)
 \exp\left(-2\Re\log\eta_D-
                   \frac{2\pi(\Im h)^2}{\Im\tau}\right),
\]
and test its upper endpoint against the exact integer 2.

All 19701 tests succeeded. The full output records each new enclosure;
the largest is enclosed by
\[
 1.999877571767410524070536478244687423578792301873142913
       \ \pm 9.26\cdot10^{-56}.
\]
This is the enclosure of a certified upper bound, not an estimate of
the actual maximum. Its box has input index 17866, with zero-based
indexing. The file digest of the input is recorded in the output.

The cover check is exact rational arithmetic. At all 438 distinct
vertical edges we maintain the active closed vertical intervals. In
every open vertical slab they form an ordered partition of
$[17/20,2]$, each with multiplicity one. The last active set is empty;
all leaves lie in the root rectangle, and the sum of their exact areas
is $23/40$. The closed rectangles also cover their common edges.
The omitted and excluded conditions are checked separately using
rational endpoint comparisons. Finally,
$2(1/10000)^2<(3/20000)^2$ puts the entire omitted square inside the
analytic disc used below. This verifies both the inequalities and
the coverage, rather than just replaying the old list of successful
flags.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[quantitative local maximum]\label{push:src:E.4.2}
If $|\tau-i|\leq3/20000$ and $\wp_\tau(z)=0$, then
$\mathcal N(z,\tau)\leq\sqrt2$, with equality precisely at
$\tau=i$. The proof uses the explicit constants below.
\end{theorem}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and calculations in the proof}


\begin{proof}
Set $x=\tau-i$, $G(h,\tau)=\wp_\tau((1-\tau)/2+h)$ and
$H(h,\tau)=\log(\vartheta_3(h,\tau)/\eta_D(\tau))$.
Both functions are even in $h$. On $|h|\leq1/5$, $|x|\leq1/10$,
the point $(1-\tau)/2+h$ has distance at least $0.9/2-0.2$ in
imaginary part from any lattice point, so $G$ has no pole.
Put
\[
 A_k=\sum_{n\geq1}n^ke^{-0.9\pi n^2}\cosh(0.4\pi n),
 \quad a_0=2A_0,\ a_1=4\pi A_1,\ a_2=8\pi^2A_2,
 \quad r=e^{-1.8\pi}.
\]
Then $a_0<0.225$, so the theta series has no zero there and a
holomorphic logarithm exists. From
$G=-\partial_h^2\log\vartheta_3-\pi^2E_2/3$ we obtain
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 |G|&\leq\frac{a_2}{1-a_0}+
 \frac{a_1^2}{(1-a_0)^2}+
 \frac{\pi^2}{3}\left(1+\frac{24r}{(1-r)^3}\right)<18.373<20,\\
 |H|&\leq-\log(1-a_0)+\frac{1.1\pi}{12}
                  +\frac{r}{(1-r)^2}<0.547<0.6.
 \end{aligned}
\]
The new certified upper bounds are respectively
$18.372504032305989$ and $0.546229724979279$.
For the sums $A_k$ we retain ten terms. If $n=11+j$, then
$n^2\geq121+23j$ and $n^k\leq11^k(1+j)^k$; replacing cosh by
the positive exponential bounds the tail by a geometric series with
ratio $e^{-20.3\pi}$ and its first two moment sums. These formulas,
including all outward rounding, are in the accompanying program.

At $(0,i)$ the coefficients are
\[
 G=0,\qquad G_{h^2}=-g_2(i)/4,\qquad G_x=id,
 \qquad H=\log\sqrt2,\quad H_x=0,\quad H_{h^2}=-\pi/2,
\]
where $d>0$. The first two identities follow from the half-period
value of $\wp$ and $\wp''=6\wp^2-g_2/2$. If
$e_2(\tau)=\pi^2(\vartheta_2^4-\vartheta_4^4)/3$, differentiating
its Gaussian series gives $e_2'(i)=id$. We compute
\[
 \begin{split}
 10.03&<d<10.04,\\
 47.26&<g_2(i)/4<47.30.
 \end{split}
\]
More precisely the certified enclosures begin
$d=10.03061933746602249879\ldots$ and
$g_2(i)/4=47.26818003230846307326\ldots$.
The computation of $d$ uses 16 terms in the two Gaussian series and
their derivatives, followed by geometric Gaussian tail bounds.
For $g_2/4$ it uses
\[
 \frac{g_2(i)}4=\frac{\pi^4}{3}
 \left(1+240\sum_{n\geq1}\frac{n^3e^{-2\pi n}}{1-e^{-2\pi n}}\right)
\]
with 24 terms and the bound
$\sum_{n>24}n^3q^n/(1-q^n)
\leq25^3q^{25}(1+4q+q^2)/(1-q)^5$.
The modular transformation of $\vartheta_3/\eta_D$ gives $H_x=0$;
that of eta gives $E_2(i)=3/\pi$. Inserting this in the displayed
formula for $G$ gives $H_{h^2}=-\pi/2$.

Take $\epsilon=3/20000$, $r_h=3/100$,
$s=\epsilon/(1/10)=3/2000$ and $r_2=(r_h/(1/5))^2=9/400$.
Cauchy's coefficient estimates give on $|h|=r_h$
\[
 |G(h,i)|\geq
 \left(47.26-\frac{500r_2}{1-r_2}\right)r_h^2
       >0.03217594373401534,
\]
while
\[
 |G(h,i+x)-G(h,i)|\leq
 \frac{20s}{(1-s)(1-r_2)}<0.03073664204747019.
\]
Rouch\'e's theorem therefore encloses both zeros in $|h|<r_h$.
The comparison with the total number of zeros of an elliptic function
of order two identifies these with all roots modulo the lattice.

Write $G=e_2(\tau)+h^2Q(h,\tau)$. The same Cauchy bounds imply
\[
 \left|Q+\frac{g_2(i)}4\right|
 \leq\frac{500(r_2+s/(1-s))}{1-r_2}<12.277368,
 \quad
 |e_2(\tau)-idx|\leq\frac{2000|x|^2}{1-s}.
\]
At a root, first bounding the left side of the last inequality below
and then bounding it above yields respectively
\[
 |x|<6.123343|h|^2<7|h|^2,
 \qquad |h|^2<0.000044338219<\frac1{20000}.
\]
For example the two rational majorants actually evaluated are
\[
 \frac{47.30+Q_*}{10.03-2000\epsilon/(1-s)},
 \qquad
 \frac{10.04\epsilon+2000\epsilon^2/(1-s)}{47.26-Q_*},
\]
where $Q_*=500(r_2+s/(1-s))/(1-r_2)$; both denominators are
strictly positive.

In the even power series of $H$, put
$\alpha=|x|/(1/10)\leq70|h|^2$ and
$\beta=|h|^2/(1/5)^2=25|h|^2$. After removal of its displayed
constant and linear coefficients, the remaining bivariate series is
bounded by
$0.6(\alpha^2+\alpha\beta+\beta^2)/((1-\alpha)(1-\beta))$.
The change from $1/\Im\tau$ to one in the Gaussian contributes
at most $7\pi|h|^4/(1-\epsilon)$. Thus a bound for the total
coefficient of $|h|^4$ is
\[
 \frac{0.6(70^2+25\cdot70+25^2)}
 {(1-s)(1-25/20000)}+\frac{7\pi}{1-\epsilon}
 <4399.024<5000.
\]
Since $\Re(-\pi h^2/2)-\pi(\Im h)^2=-\pi|h|^2/2$, we have
\[
 \log\mathcal N-\log\sqrt2
 \leq-\frac\pi2|h|^2+5000|h|^4
 <-\left(\frac\pi2-\frac14\right)|h|^2
\]
whenever $h\ne0$. The coefficient is greater than $1.32079632679$.
If $h=0$, the lower bound for $e_2$ forces $x=0$. This proves the
claim with all constants controlled by a second arithmetic engine.
\end{proof}

\paragraph{Completion of the independent proof of Theorem~\ref{fam:st:C.2.3}.}

\begin{proof}
The theta transformation formulas preserve $\mathcal N$ under modular
transport, lattice translation, sign, and
$(z,\tau)\mapsto(\bar z,-\bar\tau)$; hence the half modular domain
suffices. Theorems \ref{push:src:E.4.1}--\ref{push:src:E.4.2} cover its portion $\Im\tau\leq2$.
For $T=\Im\tau\geq2$, choose $|\Im z|\leq T/2$ by lattice
translation. With $b=43/100$ and $r=e^{-4\pi}$, if
$|\Im z|\geq b$ the Fourier formula gives
\[
 \left|\frac{\wp_\tau(z)}{\pi^2}+\frac13\right|
 \leq\frac1{\sinh^2(\pi b)}+
 8\left\{\frac r{(1-r)^3}
 +\frac1{2(1-r)}\left(
 \frac{e^{-2\pi}}{(1-e^{-2\pi})^2}+
 \frac{e^{-6\pi}}{(1-e^{-6\pi})^2}\right)\right\}<\frac13.
\]
Thus a zero has $|\Im z|<b$. The function
$\cosh(\pi y)e^{-\pi y^2/T}$ is increasing for $0\leq y\leq b$:
concavity and the positive endpoint value of $\tanh(\pi y)-y$
give its nonnegative logarithmic derivative. The Jacobi product now
implies
\[
 \mathcal N\leq2\cosh(\pi b)
 e^{-\pi/3-\pi b^2/2}
 \exp\left(\frac{2\cosh(2\pi b)r}{1-r}
                +\frac{r^2}{1-r^2}\right)<1.082<\sqrt2.
\]
This bound decreases with $T\geq2$. Both strict inequalities are
independently checked in \path{code/e4_cover_and_local.py}.
At $\tau=i$, $\vartheta_3(0,i)/\eta_D(i)=\sqrt2$, so equality
does occur. The period identity at the beginning of the subsection
then gives the claimed value of $M$ and
$e^{-\pi M}=6^3=216$. The invariant $j(\tau)=1728t$ sends its
unique modular equality orbit to $t=1$.
\end{proof}

\section{Invariant and arithmetic notation in the family marking}
\label{inv:notation-dictionary}

\paragraph{Base, fibres, and the two peripheral orientations.}
We use $B=\mathbb P^1_t$, $p_1=0$, $p_2=1$, $p_0=\infty$,
$\Sigma=\{p_0,p_1,p_2\}$, and $D=W+S_1+S_2$ with reduced
components. The full fibres are $f^*p_1=3S_1$, $f^*p_2=4S_2$,
and $f^*p_0=W$. A positive base loop is counterclockwise in a
holomorphic local coordinate. The analytic root deck generator is
clockwise, $s_j(g_jz)=e^{-2\pi i/m_j}s_j(z)$, with
$g_1g_2g_0=1$. The lifted positive base loop ends at the inverse deck
translate; its endpoint identification applies $g_j$. Thus its
homology action is $A_j$, not $A_j^{-1}$.
The clockwise boundary orientation used in the collar integration
is stated separately in \cref{inv:C3.2}. References there to a
peripheral generator refer to this fixed analytic generator.

\paragraph{Integral marking and coordinate order.}
The homology basis is
$(\hat\gamma,\hat u,\hat w,\hat\delta)$, and
$(\gamma,u,w,\delta)$ denotes its dual cohomology basis.
The letter $w$ in that cohomology basis is a covector, whereas the
scalar family parameter below is $e^{-\pi ic}$.
In the ordered additive coordinates $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$,
\[
 \Pi_c=\begin{pmatrix}6\mu&\tau&1&0\\
             \beta_c&\mu&0&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \beta_c=\beta^{\rm part}+c,
 \qquad (\beta^{\rm part}+\tau)(p_0)=0.
\]
Its rows are $\sigma_1=6\mu\gamma+\tau u+w$ and
$\sigma_2=\beta_c\gamma+\mu u+\delta$.
The actual monodromy matrices in this column basis are
\[
 A_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\6&0&1&0\\-6&-1&-1&0\\-2&1&0&1\end{pmatrix},
 \quad
 A_2=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\0&0&-1&0\\-6&1&0&0\\3&0&1&1\end{pmatrix},
 \quad A_0=(A_1A_2)^{-1}.
\]
No row interchange is implicit: if a local calculation orders the
coordinates as $(\zeta_2,\zeta_1)$, its period matrix is
$J\Pi_c$, $J=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$,
and its Hermitian coefficient matrix is $JH J^{\mathsf t}$.
Both the main invariant proofs and the retained working-edition
fibre formulas use the displayed $(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$ order.

\paragraph{The exact Engel and reversed-meridian transitions.}
Engel's base indices $(0,1,\infty)$ correspond to $(1,2,0)$ here.
Writing his common integral basis as column coordinates, the family
basis is given by the columns of
\[
 P_{\rm mark}=\begin{pmatrix}
 0&-2&-1&-2\\2&-1&0&-1\\0&2&1&3\\-1&0&0&0
 \end{pmatrix},\qquad
 T_0P_{\rm mark}=P_{\rm mark}A_1,\quad
 T_1P_{\rm mark}=P_{\rm mark}A_2.
\]
The invariant source's reversed-meridian matrix is
\[
 Q=P_{\rm mark}S,\qquad
 S=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0&0\\-6&0&-1&0\\6&-1&0&0\\2&1&1&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 Q=\begin{pmatrix}2&-1&0&-2\\2&-1&0&-1\\0&2&1&3\\1&0&0&0\end{pmatrix}.
\]
It satisfies $T_0Q=QA_1^{-1}$ and $T_1Q=QA_2^{-1}$.
This is the explicit convention change of \cref{inv:B1.0}.
For invariant finite twist vectors $v_1,v_2$, Engel's positive-root
affine vectors are $a_0=-P_{\rm mark}v_1/3$ and
$a_1=-P_{\rm mark}v_2/4$; his distinguished cycle is
$P_{\rm mark}\hat\delta$.

\paragraph{Multiplicative parameters and special-fibre coordinates.}
Set $v=e^{2\pi i\zeta_2}$. The first period acts by
$(\zeta_1,v)\mapsto(\zeta_1+6\mu,e^{2\pi i\beta_c}v)$.
Engel's contracting generator is its inverse over $-6P$, on the
complement of the zero section of $\mathcal O(P-O)$.
With the reference inverse lift transported from $c=0$,
\[
 w=e^{-\pi ic},\qquad u_{\rm Engel}=w^2,
 \qquad 0<|w|<216,\quad 0<|u_{\rm Engel}|<46656.
\]
A different reference lift multiplies $u_{\rm Engel}$ by a fixed
$\lambda_0\in\mathbb C^*$. Thus $u_{\rm Engel}$ is distinct from
the integral covector $u$ and from an elliptic logarithm denoted $u$
in the period-transcendence section.
The special values use $\rho=e^{\pi i/3}$ rather than
$e^{2\pi i/3}=\rho-1$; the two conventions differ by the modular
translation $\tau\mapsto\tau+1$. The Albanese parameters and their
upper-half-plane representatives are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
 &\kappa&\text{upper-half-plane period}&\text{nome}\\\hline
 S_1&c+\frac12-\frac{3i}{2\pi}\log48&-\kappa_1&
             q_1=e^{-2\pi i\kappa_1}=-w^2/48^3\\
 S_2&c+\frac32-\frac{3i}{\pi}\log6&-\kappa_2/2&
             q_2=e^{-\pi i\kappa_2}=iw/216.
 \end{array}
\]
The factor $1/2$ is the full order-four Albanese lattice projection.
In particular $q_1=(27/64)q_2^2$.

\paragraph{Determinants, orientations, and cohomology generators.}
Write $y=\Im\tau>0$, $m=\Im\mu$, $r=\Im\beta_c$, and
$D_c=r-6m^2/y=D_{\rm part}+\Im c$. The symbol $\Delta$ used
for this real quantity in the invariant fibre formulas means $D_c$,
not a Weierstrass discriminant. In admissible fibres $D_c<0$.
The real period determinant in the row order
$(\Re\zeta_1,\Im\zeta_1,\Re\zeta_2,\Im\zeta_2)$ is $yD_c$.
Consequently the marked real orientation is opposite to the complex
orientation, and for
$\eta_F=u\wedge w+6\gamma\wedge\delta$,
\[
 \int_{F,\operatorname{or}_{\mathbb C}}\eta_F^2=-12,
 \qquad
 \Gamma=\frac{i}{2D_c}
       \left(d\bar\zeta_2-\frac myd\bar\zeta_1\right)
       \quad\text{represents }\gamma^{0,1}.
\]
The subscript on $\eta_F$ separates this integral fibre class from
Dedekind's eta function and from Weierstrass quasi-periods.
The primitive global class is $\mathfrak g=g_\gamma$.
For standard data $(l_0,l_1,l_2)=(0,1,-1)$ and
$p=12l_0-4l_1-3l_2=-1$,
\[
 \exp(12\mathfrak g)=f^*\mathcal O_B(1),\quad
 \mathcal O_X(S_1-S_2)=\exp(\mathfrak g),\quad
 [G_0]=12\mathfrak g.
\]
In general the first equality is
$\exp(12g_\gamma)=f^*\mathcal O_B(-p)$.
Here $\exp$ means the sheaf map $z\mapsto e^{2\pi iz}$,
$\int_B\omega_{FS}=1$, $c_{1,BC}(L)=[iF_L/(2\pi)]$, and the
unnormalized Chern--Ricci form represents $2\pi c_{1,BC}(T_X)$.
Thus the prescribed Chern--Ricci form is $\pi f^*\omega_{FS}$.

\paragraph{Root and coarse line bundles.}
For the root curve $\mathcal B$ of orders $(3,4)$ put
$R=R_1R_2^{-1}$, so
$R_1=R^4$, $R_2=R^3$, $\rho^*\mathcal O_B(1)=R^{12}$,
and $K_{\mathcal B}=R^{-7}$.
The notation $\mathcal O_{\mathcal B}(n)$ means $R^n$;
$\mathcal O_B(n)$ is the ordinary coarse degree-$n$ line bundle.
They have different degrees and stabilizer characters.
The logarithmic sheaves are
$\mathcal L=\Omega_B^1(\log\Sigma)$,
$\mathcal A=\Omega_X^1(\log D)$, and
$\mathcal E=\mathcal A/f^*\mathcal L$.
Every coherent base-change assertion uses the full scheme fibre.
The finite cyclic covers and subsequent invariant functor retain its
nilpotent normal directions.

\paragraph{Theta norm, modular coordinate, and heights.}
The theta variable has periods $(1,\tau)$; software using a first
argument of period $\pi$ receives $\pi z$. With $q=e^{2\pi i\tau}$,
\[
 N(z,\tau)=\left|\frac{\vartheta_1(z,\tau)}{\eta(\tau)}\right|
       e^{-\pi(\Im z)^2/\Im\tau},\qquad
 D_{\rm part}=\frac6\pi\log\frac{N(\mu,\tau)}{2\sqrt3},
 \qquad t=\frac{j(\tau)}{1728}.
\]
The modular discriminant is
$\Delta_0=q\prod_{n\ge1}(1-q^n)^{24}$, so
$t=E_4^3/(1728\Delta_0)$ and $t-1=E_6^2/(1728\Delta_0)$.
For the rational family
\[
 E_t:Y^2=X^3-\tfrac34t^3(t-1)X+\tfrac14t^4(t-1)^2,
 \qquad P_t=(0,t^2(t-1)/2),
\]
the invariant differential is $dX/(2Y)$ and
$\Delta_E=27t^8(t-1)^3$.
In the lattice model $X=\wp(u)$ and $Y=\wp'(u)/2$;
the lattice discriminant is
$g_2^3-27g_3^2=(2\pi)^{12}\eta(\tau)^{24}$ when the
period lattice is $\mathbb Z+\tau\mathbb Z$.
We use the height of $(O)$,
$\widehat h_O(P)=\frac12\lim n^{-2}h(x(nP))$.
PARI's \texttt{ellheight}, the surface self-pairing, and the
rank-one BSD regulator use $2\widehat h_O$.
The full real period is $\Omega=\int_{E(\mathbb R)}|\omega|$,
including both components if disconnected.
The archimedean local height is exactly $-\log N$.
At finite places $|p|_v=p^{-1}$ and $n_v=[K_v:\mathbb Q_p]$;
complex embeddings are counted separately in the global sum.

For period arguments, $\eta_j$ is defined by
$\zeta(z+\omega_j)=\zeta(z)+\eta_j$, with
$\omega_1\eta_2-\omega_2\eta_1=-2\pi i$.
The real-linear extension of these quasi-periods is denoted $\eta(u)$.
In the critical-point proof, the Cayley coordinate is
$\chi=(\tau-i)/(\tau+i)$, $z=k\chi^2$, and
$\beta_{\rm cusp}=\log(5+2\sqrt6)/(2\pi)$;
neither symbol is the family parameter $w$ or the period $\beta_c$.

\paragraph{Shared statements.}
The maximum has the single label \cref{fam:src:C.2.3}, with aliases
\texttt{ari:C.8.5} and \texttt{push:src:E.4.3}; the independent

The exact parameter classification is \cref{fam:src:A.5.1};
the canonical-pencil statement is \cref{fam:src:A.1.1}.
The working Hodge-line proof is \cref{mapsI:hodge:line},
and the finite normal-order calculation is

Working structure-sheaf and cusp statements share \cref{inv:A1.0};

the Bott--Chern multiplication statement shares \cref{inv:C3.3}.

\section{The analytic threefold constructed in the candidate}
\label{wb:sec:candidate-geometry}

This section audits the construction itself.  It does not infer existence
from the later topology.  The period family, the three local fillings, and
the gluing are proved in that order.  The notation is the candidate's:
\(B\simeq\mathbb P^1\),
\(B^\circ=B\setminus\{p_0,p_1,p_2\}\), and the local monodromy orders at
\(p_1,p_2\) are \(m_1=3,m_2=4\).

\subsection{The period family}

Let \(\Delta\simeq(\mathbb Z/3)*(\mathbb Z/4)\) be the orientation-preserving
\((3,4,\infty)\)-triangle group acting on a simply connected Riemann surface
\(\mathfrak h_z\), with elliptic generators \(g_1,g_2\) and
\(g_0=(g_1g_2)^{-1}\).  Let \(t\) be the affine coordinate on
\(B\) with values \(0,1,\infty\) at \(p_1,p_2,p_0\), respectively.
Write
\[
 \pi:\mathfrak h_z\longrightarrow B\setminus\{p_0\}
\]
for the orbifold quotient map; its stabilizers at chosen lifts
\(z_j\in\pi^{-1}(p_j)\) are \(\langle g_j\rangle\).  Let
\(\rho_V:\Delta\to\operatorname{GL}(V)\) be the printed representation,
\(\rho_V(g_j)=T_j\), and put
\[
 M_g:=\rho_V(g)^{\mathsf t},\qquad A_g:=M_g^{-1}.
\]
Thus \(M_{gh}=M_hM_g\), \(A_{g_j}=A_j\), and
\(A_{g_0}=M_0\) in the notation of \cref{wb:prop:monodromy-certificate}.

\begin{lemma}[simultaneous elliptic-orientation normalization]
\label{wb:lem:triangle-generator-orientations}
\ The generators may, and henceforth do, satisfy
\begin{equation}
 g_1'(z_1)=e^{-2\pi i/3},\qquad
 g_2'(z_2)=e^{-2\pi i/4}=-i,
\label{wb:eq:triangle-generator-derivatives}
\end{equation}
while \(g_0=(g_1g_2)^{-1}\) remains parabolic.  More precisely, the Cayley
coordinates
\begin{equation}
 s_j(z)=\frac{z-z_j}{z-\bar z_j}
\label{wb:eq:triangle-cayley-coordinates}
\end{equation}
obey
\begin{equation}
 s_1\circ g_1=e^{-2\pi i/3}s_1,
 \qquad
 s_2\circ g_2=-is_2.
\label{wb:eq:triangle-linearizing-identities}
\end{equation}
The two signs in \cref{wb:eq:triangle-generator-derivatives} are a simultaneous
orientation choice; they are not obtained by shrinking a coordinate disc.
\end{lemma}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cite[Section~7.38 and Section~10.6 (the latter checked in the 1986 translation)]{Beardon1983}}


\begin{proof}
Realize \(\Delta\) as the orientation-preserving subgroup of the reflection
group of a hyperbolic triangle with counterclockwise vertices \(A,B,C\),
angles \(\pi/3,\pi/4,0\), and opposite sides \(a,b,c\), respectively.  Let
\(\sigma_a,\sigma_b,\sigma_c\) denote reflection in those sides and put
\[
 x=\sigma_b\sigma_c,\qquad
 y=\sigma_c\sigma_a,\qquad
 z=\sigma_a\sigma_b.
\]
The product of reflections in two oriented geodesics meeting at angle
\(\theta\) is the rotation through \(2\theta\).  Hence \(x\) is the
counterclockwise rotation about \(A\) through \(2\pi/3\), \(y\) is the
counterclockwise rotation about \(B\) through \(\pi/2\), and \(z\) is
parabolic at the ideal vertex \(C\); this is the standard triangle-group
construction \cite[Section~7.38 and Section~10.6 (the latter checked in the 1986 translation)]{Beardon1983}.  Moreover
\[
 xyz=\sigma_b\sigma_c\sigma_c\sigma_a\sigma_a\sigma_b=1.
\]
Set
\[
 z_1=A,\qquad z_2=B,\qquad g_1=x^{-1},\qquad g_2=y^{-1}.
\]
Both finite rotations are thereby reversed, so their complex derivatives at
their fixed points are exactly those in
\cref{wb:eq:triangle-generator-derivatives}.  Since
\(g_2g_1=y^{-1}x^{-1}=z\), one also has
\[
 g_1g_2=g_1zg_1^{-1};
\]
thus \(g_1g_2\), and therefore \(g_0=(g_1g_2)^{-1}\), is parabolic.

This simultaneous reversal is forced once the orientation of \(g_1\) and
the cusp conjugacy class are fixed.  Indeed, in
\(\langle x\rangle*\langle y\rangle\simeq C_3*C_4\) every parabolic element
is conjugate to a nonzero power of the primitive cusp word
\(z=y^{-1}x^{-1}=y^3x^2\).  The two mixed choices would instead give
\[
 (x^{-1}y)^{-1}=y^{-1}x=y^3x,
 \qquad
 (xy^{-1})^{-1}=yx^{-1}=yx^2.
\]
Both words are cyclically reduced of length two.  A nontrivial power
\(z^n\) has cyclically reduced length \(2|n|\); hence a mixed word could be
parabolic only for \(|n|=1\).  But neither \(y^3x\) nor \(yx^2\) is a cyclic
permutation of \(y^3x^2\) or its inverse \(xy\).  Thus neither mixed choice
is parabolic.  The derivative selected at \(z_1\) consequently fixes the
derivative at \(z_2\) as well.

Finally, for an elliptic M\"obius transformation \(g\) fixing
\(z_0\in\mathfrak h_z\), the Cayley map
\(s=(z-z_0)/(z-\bar z_0)\) conjugates \(g\) to a disc automorphism fixing
zero.  Such an automorphism is \(s\mapsto g'(z_0)s\).  Applying this to
\(g_1,g_2\) proves \cref{wb:eq:triangle-linearizing-identities}.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[existence and non-degeneracy of the period matrix]
\label{wb:prop:period-input-audit}
\ There are holomorphic functions
\[
 \tau:\mathfrak h_z\to\mathfrak h,
 \qquad \mu,\beta:\mathfrak h_z\to\mathbb C
\]
satisfying
\[
\begin{array}{lll}
\tau\circ g_0=\tau-1,&\mu\circ g_0=\mu,&\beta\circ g_0=\beta+1,\\
\tau\circ g_2=-1/\tau,&\mu\circ g_2=1+\mu/\tau,
 &\beta\circ g_2=\beta-3-6\mu^2/\tau,
\end{array}
\tag{2.1}
\]
and the corresponding order-three transformation laws obtained from
\(\tau\circ g_1=(\tau-1)/\tau\).  They may be chosen so that
\[
 \operatorname{Im}\tau>0,
 \qquad
 D:=\operatorname{Im}\beta-
 \frac{6(\operatorname{Im}\mu)^2}{\operatorname{Im}\tau}<0.
\tag{2.2}
\]
Consequently
\[
 \Pi=[Z\mid I_2],\qquad
 Z=\begin{pmatrix}6\mu&\tau\\ \beta&\mu\end{pmatrix}
\tag{2.3}
\]
maps the marked rank-four lattice \(\Lambda\) isomorphically onto a lattice
in \(\mathbb C^2\) at every point.  The quotients
\(\mathbb C^2/\Pi(z)\Lambda\) form a holomorphic family of compact
two-dimensional complex tori over \(\mathfrak h_z\), equivariant for
\(\Delta\).
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cite[Chapter~VII]{Serre1973}; \cref{wb:eq:period-deck-homomorphism}; \cref{wb:lem:triangle-generator-orientations}}


\begin{proof}
Normalize the modular function by
\(j(q)=q^{-1}(1+O(q))\) and put
\(J_B=1728(t\circ\pi)\); the modular facts used here are collected in
\cite[Chapter~VII]{Serre1973}.  Put
\[
 \mathfrak h_z^\dagger=
 \mathfrak h_z\setminus J_B^{-1}\{0,1728\},\qquad
 \mathfrak h_\tau^\dagger=
 \mathfrak h\setminus j^{-1}\{0,1728\}.
\]
Away from the deleted sets, the classical modular map
\(j:\mathfrak h_\tau^\dagger\to\mathbb C\setminus\{0,1728\}\) is an
unramified covering with deck group
\(\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\).  The deleted set in
\(\mathfrak h_z\) is locally finite.  Since \(\mathfrak h_z\) is simply
connected, \(\pi_1(\mathfrak h_z^\dagger)\) is normally generated by small
positive meridians about its points.  At a translate of \(z_1\), \(J_B\)
has local degree three over \(0\); the corresponding meridian therefore has
deck image equal to the third power of the order-three modular generator.
At a translate of \(z_2\), \(J_B\) has local degree four over \(1728\); its
meridian has deck image equal to the fourth power of the order-two modular
generator.  Both images are the identity.  The covering-space lifting
criterion gives a global lift \(\tau\) with \(j(\tau)=J_B\).

Near a deleted point, compose the lift with a biholomorphism
\(\chi:\mathfrak h\to\mathbb D\).  The bounded map \(\chi\circ\tau\)
extends by the removable-singularity theorem.  Its value at the puncture has
modulus strictly less than one: equality would give an interior maximum and
force \(\chi\circ\tau\) to be constant, although its punctured values lie in
 \(\mathbb D\).  Thus the extension still lands in \(\mathfrak h\).

Because \(J_B\) is \(\Delta\)-invariant, \(\tau\circ g\) and \(\tau\) are
lifts of the same map through the Galois covering \(j\) on the punctured
surface.  Hence there is a unique deck transformation
\(\varphi(g)\in\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \tau\circ g=\varphi(g)\circ\tau.
\label{wb:eq:period-deck-homomorphism}
\end{equation}
The identity extends across the deleted points.  Uniqueness and
\((\tau\circ g)\circ h=\tau\circ(gh)\) give
\(\varphi(gh)=\varphi(g)\varphi(h)\), so \(\varphi\) is a homomorphism.

Normalize \(\tau(z_1)=\rho=e^{\pi i/3}\).  The local cubic expansion of
\(j\) at \(\rho\), together with the local degree three of \(J_B\), gives a
simple zero of \(\tau-\rho\) at \(z_1\).  At \(z_2\), choose
\(\gamma\in\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) with
\(\tau(z_2)=\gamma(i)\).  The local quadratic expansion of
\(j\circ\gamma\) at \(i\), together with the local degree four of \(J_B\),
 gives a double zero of \(\gamma^{-1}\tau-i\) at \(z_2\).  At \(z_1\),
 differentiating \cref{wb:eq:period-deck-homomorphism} and using the simple
 zero gives
 \[
  \varphi(g_1)'(\rho)=g_1'(z_1)=e^{-2\pi i/3}.
 \]
 The stabilizer of \(\rho\) is generated by
 \(S_1(\tau)=(\tau-1)/\tau\), whose derivative at \(\rho\) is
 \(e^{-2\pi i/3}\); hence \(\varphi(g_1)=S_1\), rather than \(S_1^{-1}\).
 The order-four generator cannot have trivial modular image:
otherwise the invariant local power series \(\gamma^{-1}\tau-i\) would have
order divisible by four, contrary to its order two.  Its modular image
 therefore has order two.  If \(P=\varphi(g_0)\), the exact relation
 \(g_1g_2g_0=1\) gives
 \begin{equation}
  \varphi(g_2)=S_1^{-1}P^{-1}.
 \label{wb:eq:period-second-generator-from-cusp}
 \end{equation}

It remains to determine the cusp image.  Choose a punctured cusp disc
\(D_0^*\subset B\) and a component
\[
 U_0\subset\pi^{-1}(D_0^*)
\]
stabilized by \(\langle g_0\rangle\).  Choose \(R\) and shrink \(D_0^*\) so
that \(\tau(U_0)\) lies in a single component
\[
 K\subset j^{-1}(\{|w|>R\}).
\]
Put \(P=\varphi(g_0)\).  Since \(g_0U_0=U_0\),
\[
 P\tau(U_0)=\tau(g_0U_0)=\tau(U_0).
\]
Hence \(P(K)=K\): the two components \(K\) and \(P(K)\) intersect in the
nonempty set \(\tau(U_0)\).  Let \(c\) be the rational boundary cusp of
\(K\), choose
\(\gamma_0\in\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) with
\(\gamma_0(\infty)=c\), and set
\[
 \tau'=\gamma_0^{-1}\tau|_{U_0},\qquad
 P'=\gamma_0^{-1}P\gamma_0.
\]
Then
\[
 \tau'\circ g_0=P'\circ\tau',
\]
and \(P'\) preserves \(K'=\gamma_0^{-1}K\), whose boundary cusp is
\(\infty\).

Suppose \(P'=1\).  Then \(\tau'\) is \(g_0\)-invariant and descends to a
holomorphic map \(\bar\tau':D_0^*\to\mathfrak h\).  Put
\[
 q'=\exp(2\pi i\bar\tau').
\]
After increasing \(R\), the \(q\)-expansion is valid on \(K'\), and
\(0<|q'|<1\).  Thus \(q'\) extends holomorphically across the puncture.
If \(|q'(0)|=1\), the maximum-modulus principle makes \(q'\), hence
\(J_B\), constant.  If \(q'(0)\ne0\), the expansion
\(j(q')=(q')^{-1}(1+O(q'))\) makes \(J_B\) bounded, contrary to its pole.
Therefore \(q'(0)=0\).  But a holomorphic zero has positive winding on a
small positive circle, while \(q'\) has the single-valued holomorphic
logarithm \(2\pi i\bar\tau'\) on \(D_0^*\), so its winding is zero.  This
contradiction proves \(P'\ne1\).  Since \(P'\) preserves the selected cusp
component \(K'\), it is parabolic; hence the original \(P\) is a nontrivial
parabolic.

We now discard the auxiliary conjugation by \(\gamma_0\) and return to the
original normalization
\[
 \tau(z_1)=\rho,\qquad \varphi(g_1)=S_1.
\]
Choose the trace-\(+2\) lift
\(\widetilde P\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)\) of \(P\).  For a
primitive fixed vector \((p,r)^{\mathsf t}\), it has the unique form
\[
 \widetilde P
 =I+k\begin{pmatrix}-pr&p^2\\-r^2&pr\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad p,r\in\mathbb Z,\quad \gcd(p,r)=1,\quad k\ne0.
\]
With
\[
 \widetilde S_1=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
one has
\[
 \operatorname{tr}(\widetilde S_1^{-1}\widetilde P^{-1})
 =1+k(p^2-pr+r^2).
\]
Since \(S_1^{-1}P^{-1}=\varphi(g_2)\) has projective order two, this trace
is zero.  Hence
\[
 -k(p^2-pr+r^2)=1,
\]
so \(k=-1\) and \(p^2-pr+r^2=1\).  Modulo simultaneous sign, the three
solutions are cycled transitively by \(S_1\).  Conjugating the entire deck
representation by a suitable power of \(S_1\), which fixes \(\rho\) and
leaves \(S_1\) unchanged, therefore gives
\[
 P(w)=w-1,\qquad \varphi(g_2)(w)=-\frac1w.
\]
Rename the resulting period map \(\tau\).  Since \(z_2\) is fixed by the
order-four generator, the new normalization has \(\tau(z_2)=i\), and the
preceding local ramification calculation says exactly that \(\tau-i\) has
order two at \(z_2\).  Let \(t_c\) vanish at \(p_0\) and define anew
\[
 q=e^{2\pi i\tau}.
\]
Since \(\tau\circ g_0=\tau-1\), \(q\) descends to \(D_0^*\).  The simple
pole of \(J_B=j(\tau)\) gives
\[
 q=t_cu_1(t_c),\qquad u_1(0)\ne0.
\]

Writing
\[
 S_1(w)=\frac{w-1}{w},\qquad S(w)=-\frac1w,
 \qquad P(w)=w-1,
\]
the normalized deck certificate is therefore
\begin{equation}
 \varphi(g_1)=S_1,\qquad
 \varphi(g_2)=S,\qquad
 \varphi(g_0)=P,\qquad
 S_1SP=1
 \quad\text{in }\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z).
\label{wb:eq:period-deck-certificate}
\end{equation}
Differentiation at \(z_1\), where \(\tau-\rho\) has order one, gives
\(g_1'(z_1)=S_1'(\rho)=\rho^{-2}=e^{-2\pi i/3}\).  At \(z_2\), comparison
of the quadratic leading terms gives only
\[
 \bigl(g_2'(z_2)\bigr)^2=S'(i)=-1.
\]
The choice \(g_2'(z_2)=-i\), rather than \(+i\), is supplied by the
simultaneous parabolic normalization in
\cref{wb:lem:triangle-generator-orientations}; it does not follow from the
quadratic ramification calculation alone.

We now solve the two affine cocycle problems, including the orbifold and
cusp regularity which the abbreviated argument had suppressed.  Define
\(\widetilde\jmath:\Delta\times\mathfrak h_z\to\mathbb C^*\) on the
generators by
\[
 \widetilde\jmath(g_1,z)=-\tau(z),\qquad
 \widetilde\jmath(g_2,z)=\tau(z),
\]
and extend it by
\(\widetilde\jmath(gh,z)=\widetilde\jmath(g,hz)
\widetilde\jmath(h,z)\).  This is well defined: the products around the
two finite cyclic subgroups are
\[
 (-1)^3\tau\frac{\tau-1}{\tau}\frac{-1}{\tau-1}=1,
 \qquad
 \tau\left(-\frac1\tau\right)\tau\left(-\frac1\tau\right)=1.
\]
Moreover \(\widetilde\jmath(g_0,\cdot)=1\).

For an open \(U\subset B\), set
\(\widetilde U=\pi^{-1}(U\setminus\{p_0\})\).  Define
\[
 \mathcal L(U)=\left\{\nu\in\mathcal O(\widetilde U):
 \nu\circ g=\nu/\widetilde\jmath(g,\cdot)\quad(g\in\Delta)\right\}
\]
and let \(\mathcal M(U)\) be the holomorphic functions on
\(\widetilde U\) satisfying
\[
 \mu\circ g_1=\frac{1-\mu}{\tau},\qquad
 \mu\circ g_2=1+\frac\mu\tau.
 \tag{2.1a}
\]
If \(p_0\in U\), both definitions additionally require that the restriction
to the distinguished \(\langle g_0\rangle\)-invariant cusp component,
viewed as a function of \(t_c\), extend holomorphically across \(t_c=0\).
Because \(\widetilde\jmath(g_0)=1\) and \(\mu\circ g_0=\mu\), this
requirement is meaningful and is stable under restriction.  Thus
\(\mathcal L\) is a line sheaf and \(\mathcal M\), if locally nonempty, is
an affine \(\mathcal L\)-torsor.

Local nonemptiness is explicit.  Over an ordinary small disc, prescribe
\(\mu=0\) on one sheet and extend using (2.1a).  At the cusp prescribe
\(\mu=0\) on the distinguished component.  At the elliptic points use
\[
 \mu_1=\frac{2-\tau}{3}\quad\hbox{on }\Delta_1,
 \qquad
 \mu_2=\frac{1-\tau}{2}\quad\hbox{on }\Delta_2.
 \tag{2.1b}
\]
Indeed
\[
 \mu_1\circ g_1=\frac{\tau+1}{3\tau}
 =\frac{1-\mu_1}{\tau},
 \qquad
 \mu_2\circ g_2=\frac{\tau+1}{2\tau}
 =1+\frac{\mu_2}{\tau}.
\]
The cyclic products above, or direct iteration of (2.1a), show that these
prescriptions close after three and four steps.

To identify \(\mathcal L\), use that \(E_6\) has a simple zero at the
order-two elliptic orbit and no other zero in \(\mathfrak h\).  Since
\(\tau-i\) has order two at every translate of \(z_2\), the function
\(E_6\circ\tau\) has only even-order zeros on the simply connected surface
\(\mathfrak h_z\).  Fix a holomorphic square root \(h\),
\(h^2=E_6\circ\tau\), and put
\[
 \Theta=\frac{(E_4\circ\tau)^2h}{\Delta_{\rm mod}\circ\tau}.
\]
For \(j=1,2\), the quotient
\(h(g_jz)/(\tau(z)^3h(z))\) has square one away from its removable zero
set, hence is a constant sign.  At \(z_1\), \(h(z_1)\ne0\) and
\(\rho^3=-1\), so the sign for \(g_1\) is \(-1\).  At \(z_2\), choose the
linearizing coordinate with \(s_2\circ g_2=-is_2\).  The function \(h\) has
a simple zero there, and therefore
\(h(g_2z)/h(z)\to-i=i^3\); the sign for \(g_2\) is \(+1\).  The modular
transformation formulae
\[
 E_4(\gamma\tau)=(c\tau+d)^4E_4(\tau),\quad
 E_6(\gamma\tau)=(c\tau+d)^6E_6(\tau),\quad
 \Delta_{\rm mod}(\gamma\tau)=(c\tau+d)^{12}\Delta_{\rm mod}(\tau)
\]
now give the exact identities
\[
 \Theta\circ g_1=-\Theta/\tau,\qquad
 \Theta\circ g_2=\Theta/\tau.
 \tag{2.1e}
\]
These are precisely the automorphy laws defining \(\mathcal L\).  Since
\(E_4\) has a simple zero at \(\rho\), whereas \(E_6\) has a simple zero
at \(i\), the orders of \(\Theta\) at \(z_1,z_2\) are respectively two
and one.  At the distinguished cusp, \(E_4,E_6\) are units and
\(\Delta_{\rm mod}=q\cdot(\text{unit})\), with
\(q=t_c\cdot(\text{unit})\), so
\(\Theta=t_c^{-1}\cdot(\text{unit})\).
Taking the stabilizer orders into account, division by \(\Theta\) identifies
the ordinary and elliptic stalks with \(\mathcal O_B\), while the cusp stalk
is \(\mathfrak m_{p_0}\Theta\).  Hence
\[
 \mathcal L\simeq\mathcal O_B(-p_0)\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1).
\]
Consequently \(H^1(B,\mathcal L)=H^0(B,\mathcal L)=0\): the locally
nonempty torsor \(\mathcal M\) has a unique global section.  Evaluating at
the fixed points gives
\[
 \mu(z_1)=\frac{2-\rho}{3},\qquad
 \mu(z_2)=\frac{1-i}{2},
\]
and the cusp condition says precisely that its invariant branch extends
holomorphically.

For the second affine problem put
\[
 \phi_1=2-\frac{6(1-\mu)^2}{\tau},\qquad
 \phi_2=-3-\frac{6\mu^2}{\tau}.
\]
Substitution around the finite orbits gives
\[
 \sum_{k=0}^{2}\phi_1\circ g_1^k=0,
 \qquad
 \sum_{k=0}^{3}\phi_2\circ g_2^k=0.
 \tag{2.1c}
\]
For example, the three summands in the first identity are
\[
2-\frac{6(1-\mu)^2}{\tau},\quad
2-\frac{6(\tau-1+\mu)^2}{\tau(\tau-1)},\quad
2+\frac{6\mu^2}{\tau-1},
\]
 Putting them over the common denominator \(\tau(\tau-1)\), the three
 constant terms contribute \(6\tau(\tau-1)\), while the remaining terms
 contribute \(-6\tau(\tau-1)\); hence the total numerator is zero.  For the
 order-four identity the
bracket after extracting \(6/\tau\) is \(2\tau\), cancelling \(-12\).

Define \(\mathcal B(U)\) to consist of holomorphic \(\beta\) on
\(\widetilde U\) with
\(\beta\circ g_j-\beta=\phi_j\); at the cusp require
\(b=\beta+\tau\) to extend holomorphically in \(t_c\).  Differences of
sections are ordinary holomorphic functions on \(U\), so
\(\mathcal B\) is a pseudo-torsor under \(\mathcal O_B\).  It is locally
nonempty: prescribe \(\beta=0\) on one ordinary sheet; prescribe
\(\beta=-\tau\) on the distinguished cusp component; and at \(p_j\) use
\[
 \beta_j=\frac1{m_j}\sum_{k=0}^{m_j-1}
 k\,(\phi_j\circ g_j^k).
 \tag{2.1d}
\]
Equation (2.1c) makes the last expression telescope to
\(\beta_j\circ g_j-\beta_j=\phi_j\).  Therefore \(\mathcal B\) is an
\(\mathcal O_B\)-torsor.  Since \(H^1(B,\mathcal O_B)=0\), it has global
sections, and any two differ by a constant; by construction
\(b=\beta+\tau\) is invariant and holomorphic at the cusp.

The real determinant is
\[
 \det_{\mathbb R}\Pi=-\det\operatorname{Im}Z
 =\operatorname{Im}\tau\,D.
\tag{2.4}
\]
For completeness, the equivariance can be checked before any quotient is
taken.  Regard the rows of \(\Pi\) as the two covectors
\[
 \sigma_1=6\mu\gamma+\tau u+w,
 \qquad
 \sigma_2=\beta\gamma+\mu u+\delta
 \quad\text{in }V\otimes\mathbb C.
 \tag{2.3a}
\]
Multiplication by the printed matrices gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_1\sigma_1&=(6\mu-6)\gamma+(1-\tau)u-\tau w,\\
T_1\sigma_2&=(\beta+2)\gamma+(1-\mu)u+(1-\mu)w+\delta,\\
T_2\sigma_1&=(6\mu+6\tau)\gamma-u+\tau w,\\
T_2\sigma_2&=(\beta+6\mu-3)\gamma+u+\mu w+\delta.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.3b}
\]
Using the four affine transformation laws in (2.1a)--(2.1d), coefficient
comparison in (2.3b) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \sigma_1\circ g_1&=-\tau^{-1}T_1\sigma_1,
 &\sigma_2\circ g_1&=T_1\sigma_2+(1-\mu)\tau^{-1}T_1\sigma_1,\\
 \sigma_1\circ g_2&=\tau^{-1}T_2\sigma_1,
 &\sigma_2\circ g_2&=T_2\sigma_2-\mu\tau^{-1}T_2\sigma_1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{2.3c}
\]
For instance, dividing the first line of (2.3b) by \(-\tau\) gives the
coefficients \(6(1-\mu)/\tau\), \((\tau-1)/\tau\), and \(1\), exactly
those of \(\sigma_1(g_1z)\); subtracting \((1-\mu)\) times that normalized
row from \(T_1\sigma_2\) gives \(\sigma_2(g_1z)\).  The two \(g_2\)
identities follow by the same coefficient check.  Thus, with
\[
R_{g_1}=\begin{pmatrix}-1/\tau&0\\(1-\mu)/\tau&1\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
R_{g_2}=\begin{pmatrix}1/\tau&0\\-\mu/\tau&1\end{pmatrix},
\]
pairing (2.3c) with \(\lambda\in\Lambda\) gives
\[
 \Pi(gz)=R_g(z)\Pi(z)M_g.
 \tag{2.3d}
\]
Since \(M_{gh}=M_hM_g\), uniqueness of the left factor gives
\(R_{gh}(z)=R_g(hz)R_h(z)\); hence these formulae define an action, not
merely generator-wise maps.  Taking real determinants in (2.3d), using
\(\det M_g=1\) and
\(\operatorname{Im}\tau(g_jz)=\operatorname{Im}\tau/|\tau|^2\), shows
\(D(gz)=D(z)\).  At the cusp,
\[
 D=\operatorname{Im}b-\operatorname{Im}\tau-
 \frac{6(\operatorname{Im}\mu)^2}{\operatorname{Im}\tau}
 \longrightarrow-\infty.
\]
The descended function is bounded above on the complement of a cusp
neighbourhood.  Replacing \(\beta\) by \(\beta+c_0\) adds
\(\operatorname{Im}c_0\) to \(D\), so a sufficiently negative imaginary
constant makes (2.2) hold globally.  Equation (2.4) then makes \(\Pi\) a real
isomorphism everywhere.  The equivariance identity supplies the claimed
\(\Delta\)-action and completes the construction of the period family.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[exact admissible period constants]
\label{wb:prop:period-exact-admissible-constants}
Let \(\tau,\mu,\beta^{\mathrm{part}}\) be the cusp-regular functions
constructed in \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit}, with all its marked
coordinates and transformation laws retained.  The descended function
\[
 D_{\mathrm{part}}=
 \operatorname{Im}\beta^{\mathrm{part}}
 -\frac{6(\operatorname{Im}\mu)^2}{\operatorname{Im}\tau}
\]
has an attained finite maximum \(M\) on
\(B\setminus\{p_0\}\).  The exact set of constants for which
\(\beta=\beta^{\mathrm{part}}+c_0\) makes the marked real period map an
isomorphism at every point is
\[
 \{c_0\in\mathbb C:\operatorname{Im}c_0<-M\}.
\]
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit}}


\begin{proof}
The preceding proposition proves continuity on
\(B\setminus\{p_0\}\), including its elliptic points, and convergence
\(D_{\mathrm{part}}\to-\infty\) at \(p_0\).  Choose a base point
\(b_*\).  Outside a compact set containing \(b_*\), the function is
smaller than \(D_{\mathrm{part}}(b_*)-1\).  Its maximum on that compact
set is therefore its maximum on the entire base.  A constant shift gives
\(D=D_{\mathrm{part}}+\operatorname{Im}c_0\), so \(D<0\) everywhere
exactly for \(\operatorname{Im}c_0<-M\).  At equality, \(D=0\) at a
maximum point.  For \(\operatorname{Im}c_0>-M\), that point has positive
\(D\), whereas the cusp still has negative \(D\).  A path toward the
cusp contains a zero.  Since the exact ordered real determinant is
\(\operatorname{Im}\tau\,D\), these and only these excluded constants
make the period matrix singular somewhere.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[the cusp extension is essential]
For the same \(\tau,\mu,\beta\), the function
\(\widetilde\beta=\beta+i\,t\circ\pi\) is holomorphic on
\(\mathfrak h_z\) and satisfies all the same affine transformation laws,
because \(t\circ\pi\) is invariant.  However,
\(\widetilde D=D+\operatorname{Re}t\).  On the actual ray \(t=R\to+\infty\),
\(j(\tau)=1728R\) gives
\[
 q=(1728R)^{-1}(1+O(R^{-1})),\qquad
 D(R)=-\frac{\log(1728R)}{2\pi}
       +\operatorname{Im}b(0)+o(1),
 \quad b=\beta+\tau.
\]
Consequently \(\widetilde D(R)\to+\infty\), and no additive constant
makes \(\widetilde D\) negative everywhere.  This function is excluded
by the actual construction because
\(\widetilde\beta+\tau=b+i t\) has a cusp pole.  Thus holomorphic
solvability on the open base alone does not supply the required uniform
bound; the proved cusp extension supplies it.
\end{remark}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the argument and qualifications immediately following}



For the cusp filling, record the local periods explicitly.  Let \(t_c\) be
the coordinate vanishing at \(p_0\).  The simple pole of \(j\) gives
\[
 q=e^{2\pi i\tau}=t_cu_1(t_c),\qquad u_1(0)\ne0.
\]
After choosing a logarithm of \(u_1\), put
\[
 h=(2\pi i)^{-1}\log u_1,\qquad s=\tau-h,
 \qquad b=\beta+\tau.
\]
Then \(e^{2\pi is}=t_c\), \(s\circ g_0=s-1\), and \(\mu,b,h\) are
holomorphic functions of \(t_c\) at the origin.  Consequently
\[
 B_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 Z=sB_0+C(t_c),\qquad
 C(t_c)=
 \begin{pmatrix}
 6\mu(t_c)&h(t_c)\\
 b(t_c)-h(t_c)&\mu(t_c)
 \end{pmatrix},
 \tag{2.5a}
\]
and \(C\) is holomorphic on a full cusp disc.  In particular, for
\(\bar\lambda\in\bar\Lambda\simeq\mathbb Z^2\),
\[
 \exp(2\pi iZ\bar\lambda)
 =t_c^{B_0\bar\lambda}c_{\bar\lambda}(t_c),
 \qquad
 c_{\bar\lambda}(t_c)=\exp(2\pi iC(t_c)\bar\lambda).
 \tag{2.5b}
\]

\subsection{The toric filling at the cusp}

Let \(\mathcal T_{A_2}\) be the translation-invariant triangulation of
\(\mathbb R^2\) by the two triangles
\(\{v,v+e_1,v+e_2\}\) and
\(\{v+e_1,v+e_2,v+e_1+e_2\}\).  In
\(N'=\mathbb Z^2\oplus\mathbb Z\), take the cones over all cells at height
one, and denote the associated toric threefold by \(Y\).
We use the standard orbit--cone and affine-chart constructions of
\cite[Sections~1.3--1.4, pp.~15--22]{Fulton1993} and \cite[Theorem~3.2.6, pp.~119--121]{CoxLittleSchenck2011}; all nonstandard assertions caused by
the infinite fan are proved directly below.

For \(\bar\lambda\in\bar\Lambda\), define the integral linear map
\[
 \varphi_{\bar\lambda}(y,y_3)
 =(y+y_3B_0\bar\lambda,y_3).
\]
On the height-one slice this is translation by
\(B_0\bar\lambda\in\mathbb Z^2\), so it preserves the triangulation and
maps the cone over a cell \(P\) to the cone over
\(P+B_0\bar\lambda\).  It therefore induces a toric automorphism
\(\Phi_{\bar\lambda}\) of \(Y\), satisfying
\[
 \Phi_{\bar\lambda}(x,t)
 =(t^{B_0\bar\lambda}x,t)
\]
on the dense torus.  Because \(t\) and \(C(t)\) are holomorphic on the
full cusp model, multiplication by
\((c_{\bar\lambda}(t),1)\in(\mathbb C^*)^3\) defines a biholomorphism on
all of \(Y_\epsilon\).  Set
\[
 \Psi_{\bar\lambda}(p)
 =(c_{\bar\lambda}(t(p)),1)\cdot\Phi_{\bar\lambda}(p).
\]
The maps \(\Phi_{\bar\lambda}\) fix the first two cocharacter directions
and preserve \(t\), so they commute with this torus multiplication.  The
linearity of \(C(t)\bar\lambda\) gives
\(c_{\bar\lambda}c_{\bar\mu}=c_{\bar\lambda+\bar\mu}\); hence
\(\Psi_{\bar\lambda}\Psi_{\bar\mu}
=\Psi_{\bar\lambda+\bar\mu}\).  This proves, before taking any quotient,
both the holomorphic extension and the action law used below.

For a triangle \(\sigma=\{v_0,v_1,v_2\}\), let
\(\theta_i^\sigma\) be its barycentric coordinates and let
\(z_i=\chi^{m_i}\) be the coordinates dual to
\((v_i,1)\).  Set
\[
 \sigma^{(\eta)}=\{y:\theta_i^\sigma(y)>-\eta\text{ for }i=0,1,2\},
 \quad
 \mathcal U_\sigma(S)=\{|z_i|<S\text{ for all }i\}.
\]
We use the restricted charts
\[
 \mathcal U_\sigma(S,\epsilon)=\mathcal U_\sigma(S)\cap Y_\epsilon
\]
whenever a deck transformation acts on a chart.

\begin{lemma}[toric chart control]
\label{wb:lem:toric-chart-control}
For a torus point \(p=(x,t)\) with \(0<|t|<1\), put
\[
 y(p)=\frac{(\log|x_1|,\log|x_2|)}{\log|t|}.
\]
Then
\[
 p\in\mathcal U_\sigma(S)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 y(p)\in\sigma^{(\log S/|\log|t||)}.
 \tag{2.5c}
\]
The exact closed-unit-polydisc version is
\begin{equation}
 p\in\overline{\mathcal U}_\sigma(1)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \theta_i^\sigma(y(p))\ge0\ (i=0,1,2)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y(p)\in\sigma.
\label{wb:eq:cusp-closed-chart-identity}
\end{equation}
Every point of \(\{|t|<1\}\subset Y\) belongs to
\(\overline{\mathcal U}_\sigma(1)=\{|z_i|\le1\}\) for some \(\sigma\).
Consequently the sets \(\mathcal U_\sigma(2,\epsilon)\) cover \(Y_\epsilon\), and
every compact subset is contained in the union of finitely many members of
this cover.
\end{lemma}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and calculations in the proof}


\begin{proof}
Since \((y,1)=\sum_i\theta_i^\sigma(y)(v_i,1)\), duality gives
\[
 \log|z_i(p)|=\log|t(p)|\,\theta_i^\sigma(y(p)).
\]
Because \(\log|t|<0\), this is exactly (2.5c); retaining non-strict
inequalities proves the closed-unit-polydisc assertion, including triangle
edges and vertices.

For the boundary assertion let \(p\) lie in the toric orbit
\(O_{\widehat P}\) of the cone over a cell \(P\).  In a chart with
\(\sigma\supseteq P\), the coordinates corresponding to vertices of
\(P\) vanish.  On the quotient lattice
\(N'/(N'\cap\operatorname{span}\widehat P)\), the remaining coordinates
are the characters dual to the image cone \(\bar\sigma\).  Hence
\(p\in\overline{\mathcal U}_\sigma(1)\) exactly when
\(-\operatorname{Log}_{\widehat P}(p)\in\bar\sigma\).
The cones \(\bar\sigma\), for triangles \(\sigma\supseteq P\), cover the
quotient real vector space: lift a vector \(n\), choose a relative interior
point \(p_0\in P\times\{1\}\), and for sufficiently small \(u>0\) place
the height-one rescaling of \(p_0+un\) in a triangle of the locally finite
triangulation.  That triangle contains \(P\), and its quotient cone contains
\(n\).  This proves the asserted cover.  Compactness then supplies a finite
subcover.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[the cusp quotient and its central fibre]
\label{wb:thm:candidate-cusp-geometry}
\ For the period functions and holomorphic cusp matrix \(C(t)\)
constructed above, and sufficiently small \(\epsilon>0\), the maps
\[
 \Psi_{\bar\lambda}(x,t)=
 \bigl(c_{\bar\lambda}(t)t^{B_0\bar\lambda}x,t\bigr),
 \qquad
 c_{\bar\lambda}(t)=\exp(2\pi iC(t)\bar\lambda),
\tag{2.5}
\]
extend to a free properly discontinuous action of
\(\bar\Lambda\simeq\mathbb Z^2\) on
\(Y_\epsilon=\{|t|<\epsilon\}\).  The quotient
\[
 f_0:N_0=Y_\epsilon/\bar\Lambda\longrightarrow\Delta_\epsilon
\]
is a proper holomorphic map from a connected smooth complex threefold.
Its nonzero fibres are the tori of \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit}.  Its full
scheme-theoretic central fibre \(W\) is reduced and has local equations
\[
 z_0,\qquad z_0z_1,\qquad z_0z_1z_2.
\tag{2.6}
\]
The surface \(W\) is irreducible and nonnormal.  Its normalization is
\(\nu:E_0\simeq\mathrm{dP}_6\to W\), obtained by identifying opposite sides
of the toric hexagon; its double locus consists of three rational curves
through exactly two triple points.  Thus \(W\) is a normal-crossings surface,
but it is not a simple-normal-crossings divisor.  Moreover
\[
 \omega_{N_0}\simeq\mathcal O_{N_0}.
\tag{2.6a}
\]
\end{theorem}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit}; \cite[Lemma~1.2.13 and Proposition~3.1.3, pp.~28--29 and 106--107]{CoxLittleSchenck2011}; \cref{wb:lem:toric-chart-control}}


\begin{proof}
For a bounded cell \(P\), the cone over \(P\times\{1\}\) is strongly
convex, and two such cones meet in the cone over the common face of the two
cells.  The locally finite triangulation therefore defines a countable
rational fan with support
\((\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb R_{>0})\cup\{0\}\).  For the determinant
calculation, order the height-one generators of the two kinds as
\[
 ((v,1),(v+e_1,1),(v+e_2,1)),\qquad
 ((v+e_1,1),(v+e_2,1),(v+e_1+e_2,1)).
\]
Their determinants are respectively \(+1\) and \(-1\), hence have absolute
value one.  Every cone is therefore unimodular.  Here is the pairwise
affine-chart separation argument, without assuming finiteness of the fan.
For two cones \(\kappa,\kappa'\), let \(\upsilon=\kappa\cap\kappa'\)
and \(S_\kappa=\kappa^\vee\cap M'\), where \(M'=\operatorname{Hom}(N',\mathbb Z)\).
The separation lemma for cones meeting in a common face gives an integral
character \(m\) nonnegative on \(\kappa\), nonpositive on \(\kappa'\),
and zero on each exactly along \(\upsilon\)
\cite[Lemma~1.2.13 and Proposition~3.1.3, pp.~28--29 and 106--107]{CoxLittleSchenck2011}.
For \(a\in S_\upsilon\), choose an integer \(k\ge0\) large enough
that \(a+km\) is nonnegative on every ray of \(\kappa\).  On the
common face this already holds; on each other ray \(m\) is positive.
Then \(a=(a+km)+(-km)\in S_\kappa+S_{\kappa'}\).  The reverse
inclusion follows by evaluation on \(\upsilon\).  Thus the map
\[
 \mathbb C[S_\kappa]\otimes\mathbb C[S_{\kappa'}]
 \longrightarrow\mathbb C[S_\upsilon],\qquad
 \chi^a\otimes\chi^b\longmapsto\chi^{a+b}
\]
is surjective.  It identifies the gluing graph with a closed algebraic
subset of the product of these two affine charts, hence with an
analytically closed subset.  These chart products cover \(Y\times Y\),
so its diagonal is closed.  Countability of the charts supplies a
countable topological basis.  Thus \(Y\) is a
connected Hausdorff smooth complex threefold with dense torus.

If \(m_0,m_1,m_2\) is the basis dual to the height-one generators, then the
corresponding affine chart is \(\mathbb C^3\), with coordinates
\(z_i=\chi^{m_i}\), and
\[
 t=z_0z_1z_2.
\tag{2.7}
\]
Since every primitive ray generator has height one, the divisor of \(t\) is
\(\sum_vE_v\), all with multiplicity one.  Equation (2.7) proves that the
scheme-theoretic fibre \(t^{-1}(0)\) is reduced and normal crossings.
The star of a height-one vertex has rays
\(e_1,e_2,e_2-e_1,-e_1,-e_2,e_1-e_2\), the complete smooth hexagonal fan;
hence every irreducible component \(E_v\) is \(\mathrm{dP}_6\).

The local canonical trivialization is also intrinsic to this toric model.
On the dense torus put
\[
 \Omega=\frac{dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dt}{x_1x_2}.
\]
If \((z_0,z_1,z_2)\) is a unimodular toric chart, then
\[
 \bigwedge_i\frac{dz_i}{z_i}
 =\pm\frac{dx_1}{x_1}\wedge\frac{dx_2}{x_2}\wedge\frac{dt}{t},
 \qquad t=z_0z_1z_2,
\]
and therefore \(\Omega=\pm dz_0\wedge dz_1\wedge dz_2\).  It extends
holomorphically and nowhere vanishingly across every boundary chart.
For a deck transformation \(\Psi_{\bar\lambda}\), formula (2.5) gives
\(\Psi_{\bar\lambda}^*(dx_i/x_i)=dx_i/x_i+\alpha_i(t)dt\) and
\(\Psi_{\bar\lambda}^*dt=dt\); every additional term in the pullback of
\(\Omega\) contains \(dt\) twice.  Hence \(\Omega\) is invariant and descends
to a nowhere-vanishing three-form on \(N_0\), proving the intrinsic
trivialization (2.6a).  No global threefold has been invoked at this stage.

Choose a radius \(r>0\) on which the full matrix \(C(t)\) is holomorphic,
and \(0<r_1<\min(r,1)\).  Put
\[
 R(t)=-2\pi\operatorname{Im}C(t),\qquad
 M=\max_{|t|\le r_1}\|R(t)\|<\infty.
\]
Choose \(0<\epsilon<r_1\) with \(|\log\epsilon|>2M\).
At a torus point fixed by a nonzero
\(\bar\lambda\), taking logarithmic absolute values in (2.5) gives
\[
 \log|t|B_0\bar\lambda+R(t)\bar\lambda=0,
\]
impossible because \(|B_0\bar\lambda|=|\bar\lambda|\) and the first term
has more than twice the norm of the second.  On \(t=0\), a cell is translated
by \(B_0\bar\lambda\ne0\); a bounded cell cannot be fixed by a nonzero
translation.  Thus the action is free.

For proper discontinuity put
\[
 B_t=B_0+\frac{R(t)}{\log|t|}.
\]
Then \(\|B_t-B_0\|\le1/2\), so
\(|B_t\bar\lambda|\ge|\bar\lambda|/2\).  In logarithmic position
coordinates, (2.5) is
\[
 y(\Psi_{\bar\lambda}p)=y(p)+B_t\bar\lambda.
\tag{2.8}
\]
Put \(\eta_0=\log2/|\log\epsilon|\).  If
\(\Psi_{\bar\lambda}\mathcal U_\sigma(2,\epsilon)\) meets
\(\mathcal U_{\sigma'}(2,\epsilon)\), the intersection is open in
\(Y_\epsilon\) and hence contains a
point of the dense invariant torus.  By \cref{wb:lem:toric-chart-control}, for
that point \(p\) and its image \(p'\),
\[
 y(p)\in\sigma^{(\eta_0)},\qquad
 y(p')\in{\sigma'}^{(\eta_0)}.
\]
Both thickenings are bounded, so (2.8) gives
\[
 \frac12|\bar\lambda|
 \le |B_t\bar\lambda|
 =|y(p')-y(p)|
 \le \sup_{a\in{\sigma'}^{(\eta_0)},\,b\in\sigma^{(\eta_0)}}|a-b|.
\]
Thus only finitely many \(\bar\lambda\) can make this fixed pair of charts
meet.  A compact set is contained in finitely many of the charts from
\cref{wb:lem:toric-chart-control}; taking the finite union over all chart pairs
proves proper discontinuity.  Freeness and proper discontinuity give a
Hausdorff complex-manifold quotient and a holomorphic covering map.
For completeness the restricted total space is connected: every maximal
chart intersects it in
\[
 \{(z_0,z_1,z_2)\in\mathbb C^3:|z_0z_1z_2|<\epsilon\},
\]
a set star shaped about the origin.  These connected open sets meet the
common connected dense torus
\((\mathbb C^*)^2\times\{0<|t|<\epsilon\}\).  Their union
\(Y_\epsilon\), and hence its quotient, is connected.

To prove properness, fix \(\epsilon_1<\epsilon\).  Let \(\mathcal F_0\) be
the finite set of triangles meeting the closed Euclidean ball of radius
\(\sqrt2\), and put
\[
 K_0=\bigcup_{\sigma\in\mathcal F_0}
 \left(\overline{\mathcal U}_\sigma(1)
 \cap\{|t|\le\epsilon_1\}\right).
\]
This is compact.  For a torus point \(p\) with
\(0<|t(p)|\le\epsilon_1\), put \(u=B_{t(p)}^{-1}y(p)\) and choose
\(\bar\lambda\in\mathbb Z^2\) with
\(|u+\bar\lambda|_\infty\le1/2\).  Since
\(\|B_t\|\le3/2\), equation (2.8) gives
\[
 |y(\Psi_{\bar\lambda}p)|
 =|B_t(u+\bar\lambda)|
 \le\frac{3}{2\sqrt2}<\sqrt2.
\]
Choose a triangle containing this logarithmic position.  The closed-unit-
polydisc identity of \cref{wb:lem:toric-chart-control} places the translate
in the corresponding
\(\overline{\mathcal U}_\sigma(1)\subset K_0\).

For the central representatives, we prove the needed closed-polydisc
cover explicitly.  Denote the two ordered triangles at \(v\) by
\[
 L_v=(v,v+e_1,v+e_2),\qquad
 U_v=(v+e_1,v+e_2,v+e_1+e_2).
\]
On the dense orbit of \(E_0\), the characters \((1,0,0)\) and
\((0,1,0)\) give the original coordinates \(x_1,x_2\).  The coordinate
dual to \((0,0,1)\) vanishes there; the other two dual characters have
last exponent zero.  Pairing with the ordered height-one generators gives
the following restrictions of the chart coordinates.  Write
\(a=\log|x_1|\), \(b=\log|x_2|\) on this dense orbit.
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
 \sigma&(z_0,z_1,z_2)|_{E_0^{\rm tor}}&|z_i|\le1\ (i=0,1,2)\\\hline
 L_0&(0,x_1,x_2)&a\le0,\ b\le0\\
 L_{-e_1}&((x_1x_2)^{-1},0,x_2)&a+b\ge0,\ b\le0\\
 L_{-e_2}&((x_1x_2)^{-1},x_1,0)&a+b\ge0,\ a\le0\\
 U_{-e_1}&(0,x_1^{-1},x_1x_2)&a\ge0,\ a+b\le0\\
 U_{-e_2}&(x_2^{-1},0,x_1x_2)&b\ge0,\ a+b\le0\\
 U_{-e_1-e_2}&(x_2^{-1},x_1^{-1},0)&a\ge0,\ b\ge0.
\end{array}
\]
The six regions cover \(\mathbb R^2\): the first and last cover equal
signs; for \(a\ge0\ge b\), the sign of \(a+b\) selects the second or
fourth; for \(b\ge0\ge a\), it selects the third or fifth.  Equalities
are retained throughout.  Each corresponding coordinate plane meets
\(\overline{\mathcal U}_\sigma(1)\) in a compact closed bidisc
\(Q_\sigma\subset E_0\).  Their finite union is compact and hence closed
in the already Hausdorff \(Y\).  It contains \(E_0^{\rm tor}\), so it
contains its closure \(E_0\); the reverse inclusion follows from
\(Q_\sigma\subset E_0\).  Consequently
\[
 E_0=\bigcup_{\sigma\ni0}Q_\sigma.
\]
This proves the closed-polydisc cover at every boundary point as well as
on the dense orbit, without presupposing compactness of \(E_0\).

Now let \(p\) lie in the central orbit belonging to a cell \(P\), choose
a vertex \(v\in P\), and set \(\bar\lambda=B_0v\).  The exact map
\(\Psi_{B_0v}\) translates the cell to \(P-v\), because \(B_0^2v=-v\),
and retains the full torus multiplier
\[
 c_{B_0v}(0)=\exp\bigl(2\pi iC(0)B_0v\bigr).
\]
This nonzero multiplier preserves the orbit label, so the actual
translated point belongs to \(E_0\).  The proved cover applies to it
regardless of the multiplier's modulus or argument.  Each of the six
triangles contains zero and therefore belongs to \(\mathcal F_0\), so
the translate lies in \(K_0\).  Together with the nonzero-fibre
representatives above, this proves that the image of \(K_0\) in the
quotient is exactly \(f_0^{-1}(\{|t|\le\epsilon_1\})\), which is compact.
Every compact subset of the open base disc is closed in one such closed
subdisc; its inverse image is therefore closed in that compact Hausdorff
inverse image.  Thus \(f_0\) is proper.

For \(t\ne0\), choose \(s\) with \(e^{2\pi is}=t\).  The multiplier in
(2.5) is \(\exp(2\pi iZ(s)\bar\lambda)\), so exponentiation identifies the
fibre with
\[
 \mathbb C^2/(\mathbb Z^2+Z(s)\mathbb Z^2).
\]
It is compact because \(\operatorname{Im}Z(s)\) is invertible by (2.2).

The quotient map is a local biholomorphism; therefore the local equation
(2.7), its multiplicity one, and reducedness descend to \(W\).  Every cell
has a vertex, and \(B_0\bar\Lambda=\mathbb Z^2\) acts simply transitively on
vertices, so every orbit in the central fibre meets \(E_0\).  Thus
\(E_0\to W\) is surjective.  Two interior points cannot be identified; on
the boundary, precisely opposite edges and the corresponding hexagon
vertices are identified.  The fibres have at most three points.  Since
\(E_0\) is compact, the map is finite; since it is generically injective
from a smooth irreducible surface to the reduced surface \(W\), it is the
