Indeed \(\alpha_B\bar f\simeq f\alpha_A\) and \(\bar f\beta_A\simeq\beta_Bf\), by the two homotopies in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:4.3}. Substituting them in \(fh\) and \(hf\), followed by \(\bar f\bar h\simeq1\) and \(\bar h\bar f\simeq1\), gives \(fh\simeq1_B\) and \(hf\simeq1_A\). This proves the required correspondence, with both domains and codomains retained.

\subsection{The integer comparison and the original sphere maps}
\label{mapsI:pf:integral-comparison}

\begin{theorem}
\label{mapsI:pf:theorem:5.1}
Let \(f:A\to B\) be an integral homology equivalence between path-connected, simply connected spaces with specified CW homotopy comparisons. Then \(f\) is a homotopy equivalence. The construction below gives the inverse through those comparisons, rather than replacing \(f\) by an unspecified map.
\end{theorem}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:4.4}; \cref{mapsI:pf:cw-inverses}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:4.5}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.3}; \cref{mapsI:cw:hurewicz-theorem-result}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.14}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:3.1}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.2}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.3}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:3.10}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.4}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.5}}


\begin{proof}
Apply \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:4.4}. The resulting map between CW complexes is again an integral homology equivalence and both CW complexes are simply connected. It is enough to prove that this map is a weak equivalence, since \cref{mapsI:pf:cw-inverses} then supplies \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:4.5}. Denote the two CW complexes for this proof by \(A'\) and \(B'\), their map by \(f'\), its path-fibration total space by \(E\), and its fibre at the chosen vertex by \(K\). The retraction \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.3} makes \(E\) homotopy equivalent to \(A'\), and \(p_*:H_j(E)\to H_j(B')\) is an isomorphism for every \(j\).

The fibre \(K\) is path connected. To check the component assertion directly, connect any two fibre points by a path in the connected total space \(E\). Its projection is a loop in the simply connected \(B'\), so it contracts relative its endpoints. Lift this homotopy with the original path on its bottom and the two constant endpoint lifts on its sides, using the relative square. Its top is a path in \(K\) connecting the original fibre points.

Choose \(a_*\in A'\) and a path from \(f'(a_*)\) to the reference vertex of \(B'\); together they specify a point \(e_*\in K\). The retraction \(r_f\) sends that point to \(a_*\). The basepoint comparison from the constant path to the chosen path projects to exactly this chosen base path. The degree-two Hurewicz maps for \(A'\) and \(B'\) are isomorphisms and are natural, by \cref{mapsI:cw:hurewicz-theorem-result}. The homology isomorphism \(f'_*\), with this basepoint transport, consequently makes \(\pi_2(E,e_*)\to\pi_2(B',b_*)\) an isomorphism. In \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.14}, its surjectivity and \(\pi_1(E)=0\) imply

\begin{equation}
\pi_1(K)=0.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.1}
\end{equation}

Suppose \(K\) has a nonzero positive homotopy group, and let \(n\geq2\) be its least degree. First Hurewicz, which was proved for the actual path-connected space rather than only for CW spaces, gives

\begin{equation}
H_i(K)=0\quad(0<i<n),\qquad
H_n(K)\cong\pi_n(K)\ne0.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.2}
\end{equation}

Apply \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:3.1} to \(E\to B'\). For the entry \((0,n)\), an incoming page-\(r\) source is \((r,n-r+1)\). It is zero for \(2\leq r\leq n\), by \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.2}. For \(r>n+1\) its second coordinate is negative. Thus the only possible incoming differential is

\begin{equation}
d_{n+1}:E_{n+1}^{n+1,0}\longrightarrow E_{n+1}^{0,n}.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.3}
\end{equation}

There is no outgoing differential from column zero. The source in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.3} is exactly \(H_{n+1}(B')\) at that page: bottom-row entries have no incoming maps, and each earlier outgoing target from \((n+1,0)\) has fibre degree \(r-1\) between one and \(n-1\), hence is zero. For later pages its target column is negative. Therefore

\begin{equation}
E_\infty^{n+1,0}=\ker d_{n+1}\subset H_{n+1}(B').
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.4}
\end{equation}

By \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:3.10} this subgroup is the image of \(p_*:H_{n+1}(E)\to H_{n+1}(B')\). That map is surjective. Thus the kernel in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.4} is the entire source, and \(d_{n+1}=0\). It follows that

\begin{equation}
H_n(K)=E_\infty^{0,n}=F_0H_n(E).
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.5}
\end{equation}

Since \(n\geq2\), this subgroup lies in \(F_{n-1}H_n(E)=\ker p_*\), by \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:3.10}. But \(p_*:H_n(E)\to H_n(B')\) is injective. Thus \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.5} is zero, contradicting \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.2}.

There is consequently no first nonzero positive homotopy group: all of them vanish. Together with path connectivity, \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.14} says that \(p\), and hence \(f'\), induces every homotopy isomorphism. \cref{mapsI:pf:cw-inverses} gives its inverse \(\bar h\) and the original inverse \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:4.5}. Both homotopies there have already been proved. This completes the theorem.
\end{proof}

\emph{\cref{mapsI:pf:theorem:5.1}, equations \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.2}--\eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.5}. The entry \(H_n(K)\) may receive \(d_{n+1}\). Surjectivity in degree \(n+1\) first makes that map zero. Injectivity in degree \(n\) then makes the surviving fibre subgroup zero. These are the actual proved homology edge maps.}

We now apply the theorem with the exact maps and orientation classes of \cref{mapsI:course:homotopy-section}. The already proved integral and fundamental-group calculations give \(\pi_1(X)=0\) and

\begin{equation}
H_k(X;\mathbb Z)=
\begin{cases}\mathbb Z,&k=0,6,\\0,&k\ne0,6,\end{cases}
\qquad [X]\in H_6(X;\mathbb Z)
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.6}
\end{equation}

with the original complex orientation. Successive applications of first Hurewicz give \(\pi_2(X)=\cdots=\pi_5(X)=0\), then an isomorphism \(h_6:\pi_6(X)\to H_6(X;\mathbb Z)\). Choose \(g:S^6\to X\) representing \(h_6^{-1}[X]\). Its positive sphere class satisfies

\begin{equation}
g_*[S^6]=[X].
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.7}
\end{equation}

This makes \(g\) an integral homology equivalence in every degree. Retain the actual maps of \cref{mapsI:cw:cw-manifolds},

\begin{equation}
\alpha_X:T_X\to X,\quad\beta_X:X\to T_X,\qquad
\alpha_X\beta_X=1_X,\quad\beta_X\alpha_X\simeq1_{T_X}.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.8}
\end{equation}

For \(\bar g=\beta_Xg:S^6\to T_X\), \cref{mapsI:pf:theorem:5.1} and \cref{mapsI:pf:cw-inverses} supply \(\bar h:T_X\to S^6\). The inverse to the original \(g\) is

\begin{equation}
h_X=\bar h\beta_X:X\to S^6,\qquad
h_Xg\simeq1_{S^6},\qquad gh_X\simeq1_X.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.9}
\end{equation}

For the second equality, use \(g=\alpha_X\bar g\) exactly, then \(\bar g\bar h\simeq1_{T_X}\), then \(\alpha_X\beta_X=1_X\). Thus the orientation degree in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.7} has not been replaced or rescaled.

For the cobordism, retain the two original disjoint orientation-preserving coordinate disks, their radii \(R_0,R_1\), and

\begin{equation}
C=X\setminus(\operatorname{int}D_0\cup\operatorname{int}D_1),
\qquad i_j:\partial D_j\hookrightarrow C.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.10}
\end{equation}

Excision for the original two discs and the integral homology of \(X\) give the actual pair sequence

\begin{equation}
0\longrightarrow H_6(C)\longrightarrow
\mathbb Z[X]\xrightarrow{\,1\mapsto(1,1)\,}
\mathbb Z[D_0,\partial D_0]\oplus\mathbb Z[D_1,\partial D_1]
\xrightarrow{\partial}H_5(C)\longrightarrow0.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.11}
\end{equation}

Consequently \(H_6(C)=0\), \(H_5(C)=\mathbb Z^2/\mathbb Z(1,1)\), and the two actual boundary classes are the opposite generators \([(1,0)]\) and \([(0,1)]=-[(1,0)]\). The remaining positive homology groups vanish. Van Kampen gives \(\pi_1(C)=0\), by adding the two simply connected discs back along collars of their simply connected boundary spheres, and each boundary is a simply connected \(S^5\). Each \(i_j\) is therefore an integral homology equivalence, with its own displayed sign. The CW model of \cref{mapsI:cw:cw-manifolds} for \(C\) preserves the radii in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.10}; write its maps as \(\alpha_C,\beta_C\). Applied to \(\beta_Ci_j\), the same construction yields

\begin{equation}
h_j=\bar h_j\beta_C:C\to\partial D_j,\qquad
h_ji_j\simeq1_{\partial D_j},\qquad i_jh_j\simeq1_C.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:5.12}
\end{equation}

This proves that the particular punctured manifold in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.10}, with its original two inclusions, is an \(h\)-cobordism. Equations \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.9} and \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:5.12} complete the homotopy assertions. Its smooth product structure and the extension problem for the later gluing diffeomorphism require the smooth recognition arguments; the homotopy comparison alone does not supply them.

\subsection{Two worked checks of the mechanism}
\label{mapsI:pf:path-fibre-exercises}

\begin{example}[Worked Exercise 6.1]
\label{mapsI:pf:exercise:6.1} Fix \(n\geq2\) and an integer \(m\). Take the free chain complex

\begin{equation}
C_0=\mathbb Ze,\quad C_n=\mathbb Zb,\quad C_{n+1}=\mathbb Za,
\qquad da=mb,\quad db=de=0.
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:6.1}
\end{equation}

Put \(e,b\) in filtration zero, \(a\) in filtration \(n+1\), and use the increasing filtration they generate. Compute its pages and both relevant homology maps under the quotient \(P:C\to C/\mathbb Zb\). This is an algebraic model of the edge calculation; no fibration realization is assumed.

\end{example}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:2.2}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:6.2}; \cref{mapsI:pf:theorem:5.1}}

\begin{proof}[Solution] The first and second pages have \(\mathbb Z\) at \((0,0),(0,n),(n+1,0)\) and zero elsewhere. The boundary \(da\) drops filtration by \(n+1\), so every differential before page \(n+1\) is zero. Formula \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:2.2} then gives exactly

\begin{equation}
d_{n+1}:\mathbb Z[a]\longrightarrow\mathbb Z[b],
\qquad [a]\longmapsto m[b].
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:6.2}
\end{equation}

The final entries are \(\ker(m:\mathbb Z\to\mathbb Z)\) at \((n+1,0)\), \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\) at \((0,n)\), and \(\mathbb Z\) at \((0,0)\). These agree directly with the homology of \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:6.1}.

The quotient has \(H_{n+1}(C/\mathbb Zb)=\mathbb Z[a]\) and \(H_n(C/\mathbb Zb)=0\). Its degree-\(n+1\) map has image \(\ker m\), precisely the bottom-row subgroup. If \(m\ne0\), that image is zero and is not surjective. If \(m=0\), it is surjective and the incoming differential is zero; but the degree-\(n\) map has kernel \(\mathbb Z[b]\) and is not injective. For \(m=1\) or \(m=-1\), the nonzero fibre-row entry is killed completely by the incoming differential. For all other nonzero \(m\), its surviving group is exactly \(\mathbb Z/m\mathbb Z\), retaining the full integer \(m\) and its sign in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:6.2}. This verifies why both adjacent-degree arguments in \cref{mapsI:pf:theorem:5.1} are needed.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}[Worked Exercise 6.2]
\label{mapsI:pf:exercise:6.2} Determine the additive integral homology of \(\Omega S^d\), for \(d=5\) and \(d=6\), using the proved filtration.

\end{example}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.2}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.3}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.1}; \cref{mapsI:pf:eq:6.4}}

\begin{proof}[Solution] Use \(f:\{b_*\}\to S^d\) in \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.2}. Its total space is the paths starting at \(b_*\), contracted by the homotopy after \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.3}; its fibre is \(\Omega S^d\). The fibre is path connected because \(\pi_1(S^d)=0\): a based null-homotopy of a loop is a path to the constant loop, by \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:1.1}. The sphere has its one-vertex, one-\(d\)-cell structure. With \(A_j=H_j(\Omega S^d;\mathbb Z)\), its cellular homology with these coefficients gives

\begin{equation}
E_2^{0,j}=A_j,\qquad E_2^{d,j}=A_j,
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:6.3}
\end{equation}

and no other columns. Only \(d_d:(d,j)\to(0,j+d-1)\) can be nonzero. No differential enters column \(d\), so its kernel must vanish, because the total space has no positive-degree homology. No differential leaves column zero, so its positive-degree quotients must vanish too. Thus

\begin{equation}
d_d:A_j\xrightarrow{\ \cong\ }A_{j+d-1}\quad(j\geq0).
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:6.4}
\end{equation}

The entries \(A_j\) with \(0<j<d-1\) have no incoming or outgoing differential, hence are zero. Connectivity gives \(A_0=\mathbb Z\). Induction using \eqref{mapsI:pf:eq:6.4} proves, in every degree,

\begin{equation}
H_j(\Omega S^5;\mathbb Z)=
\begin{cases}\mathbb Z,&4\mid j,\\0,&4\nmid j,\end{cases}
\qquad
H_j(\Omega S^6;\mathbb Z)=
\begin{cases}\mathbb Z,&5\mid j,\\0,&5\nmid j.\end{cases}
\label{mapsI:pf:eq:6.5}
\end{equation}

This determines the additive groups. No multiplicative structure or stable homotopy group is inferred from this calculation.
\end{proof}


% END I_paperI_course_pf_foundations

% BEGIN I_paperI_course_homotopy
\section{The orientation generator and the path-fibration proof}
\label{mapsI:course:homotopy-section}

The homotopy-sphere conclusion is classical; the following argument retains
our original map and gives the distinct path-fibration proof of the course.
The complete elementary constructions used below are printed in
\cref{mapsI:cw:section,mapsI:pf:section}.  The first Hurewicz theorem and
homological Whitehead theorem are also stated in
\cite[Theorem~4.32 and Corollary~4.33]{Hatcher2002}; we use their integral,
simply connected forms.

\begin{theorem}[the original degree-one homotopy equivalence]
\label{mapsI:course:CG-S6-07-HOMOTOPY}
For the constructed threefold, with its complex orientation, there is a
map \(g:S^6\to X\) satisfying \(g_*[S^6]=[X]\), and this particular map
is a homotopy equivalence.
\end{theorem}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{mapsI:top:prop:geometric-pi1}; \cref{mapsI:top:thm:h2-vanishing,mapsI:top:lem:cohomological-closure}; \cref{mapsI:cw:hurewicz-theorem-result}; \cref{mapsI:pf:path-lifting}; \cref{mapsI:cw:cw-manifolds}; \cref{mapsI:pf:filtered-chains,mapsI:pf:serre-homology}; \cref{mapsI:pf:cw-inverses}; \cref{mapsI:course:degree-one}}


\begin{proof}
The fundamental-group calculation in
\cref{mapsI:top:prop:geometric-pi1} gives \(\pi_1(X)=0\), and
\cref{mapsI:top:thm:h2-vanishing,mapsI:top:lem:cohomological-closure}
give the complete integral homology of the sphere.  For \(2\le n\le5\),
assume inductively that \(\pi_i(X)=0\) for \(1\le i<n\).  The integral
Hurewicz map
\[
 h_n:\pi_n(X)\longrightarrow H_n(X;\mathbb Z),
 \qquad [a]\longmapsto a_*[S^n],
\]
is then an isomorphism, by \cref{mapsI:cw:hurewicz-theorem-result}.
The target vanishes, so the induction gives \(\pi_i(X)=0\) for
\(1\le i\le5\).  In degree six choose \([g]\) mapping to the positive
orientation generator \([X]\).  Thus
\begin{equation}
 g_*[S^6]=[X].
 \label{mapsI:course:degree-one}
\end{equation}
This map induces an integral homology isomorphism in every degree:
in degrees zero and six it preserves the generators, and all remaining
groups on both sides vanish.

Replace \(g\) by its actual path fibration
\[
 E_g=\{(s,\lambda):s\in S^6,\ \lambda(0)=g(s)\},
 \qquad p(s,\lambda)=\lambda(1).
\]
The path space has the compact-open topology.  The homotopy
\((s,\lambda)\mapsto(s,u\mapsto\lambda((1-t)u))\) strongly retracts
\(E_g\) onto the constant paths, identified with \(S^6\).
Under this retraction \(p\) represents \(g\).
For clarity, the lifting formula used in \cref{mapsI:pf:path-lifting}
is the following.  Given \(H:Z\times I\to X\) and an initial lift
\((s(z),\lambda_z)\), the path at time \(t\) is
\[
 \eta_{z,t}(u)=
 \begin{cases}
 \lambda_z((1+t)u),&0\le u\le (1+t)^{-1},\\
 H(z,(1+t)u-1),&(1+t)^{-1}\le u\le1.
 \end{cases}
\]
The pieces agree at the join, their two closed domains cover the parameter
space, and compact-open adjunction proves continuity.  The last endpoint
is \(H(z,t)\), while the time-zero path is exactly \(\lambda_z\).
This proves the homotopy lifting property.  Relative cell lifting gives
the exact homotopy sequence, as proved in
\cref{mapsI:pf:path-lifting}.

For the cellular filtration use the actual comparison constructed in
\cref{mapsI:cw:cw-manifolds}:
\[
 \alpha:T_X\longrightarrow X,\qquad
 \beta:X\longrightarrow T_X,\qquad
 \alpha\beta=1_X,\qquad \beta\alpha\simeq1_{T_X}.
\]
Put \(\bar g=\beta g\), let \(\bar E=E_{\bar g}\), and write
\(\bar p(s,\lambda)=\lambda(1)\).  There is an explicit comparison
\[
 J:\bar E\longrightarrow E_g,\qquad
 J(s,\lambda)=(s,\alpha\circ\lambda),
 \qquad pJ=\alpha\bar p.
\]
Its starting point is correct because
\(\alpha\beta g(s)=g(s)\), exactly.  Both total spaces retract onto the
same \(S^6\), and \(J\) commutes with these retractions.  The base
\(T_X\) is an actual simply connected CW complex with \(\pi_2(T_X)=0\).
The map \(\bar p\) is an integral homology isomorphism in every degree,
since \(\bar g=\beta g\) is one.  Let \(K\) be its fibre over a vertex.
It is path connected: a path between two fibre points in the connected
total space projects to a null-homotopic loop, and lifting its contraction
relative to the two endpoints changes that path to one in the fibre.
The exact sequence, together with \(\pi_2(T_X)=0\) and
\(\pi_1(\bar E)=\pi_1(S^6)=0\), then gives \(\pi_1(K)=0\).

Suppose a positive homotopy group of \(K\) is nonzero and choose the least
such degree \(n\ge2\).  Hurewicz gives
\[
 H_i(K;\mathbb Z)=0\quad(0<i<n),\qquad
 H_n(K;\mathbb Z)\cong\pi_n(K)\ne0.
\]
The integral homology spectral sequence for \(\bar p\), constructed
with its actual edge maps in \cref{mapsI:pf:filtered-chains,mapsI:pf:serre-homology},
has constant coefficient systems because the base is simply connected.
In total degree \(n\), the only possibly nonzero terms are
\[
 E_2^{0,n}=H_n(K),\qquad E_2^{n,0}=H_n(T_X).
\]
No differential leaves column zero.  A differential entering \((0,n)\)
has source \((r,n-r+1)\).  The sources for \(2\le r\le n\) vanish by
the displayed fibre-homology vanishings, and for \(r>n+1\) they have
negative second degree.  The sole possible incoming map is therefore
\[
 d_{n+1}:E_{n+1}^{n+1,0}\longrightarrow E_{n+1}^{0,n}.
\]
The source is still \(H_{n+1}(T_X)\): there are no incoming maps to
the bottom row, and all earlier outgoing targets have fibre degree
between one and \(n-1\).  The actual edge image
\(\operatorname{im}(\bar p_*:H_{n+1}(\bar E)\to H_{n+1}(T_X))\)
is \(E_\infty^{n+1,0}=\ker d_{n+1}\).  Surjectivity of \(\bar p_*\)
makes this kernel the whole source, so \(d_{n+1}=0\).
Consequently
\[
 H_n(K)=E_\infty^{0,n}=F_0H_n(\bar E).
\]
The other actual edge map \(\bar p_*:H_n(\bar E)\to H_n(T_X)\)
kills this first filtration subgroup: its kernel is
\(F_{n-1}H_n(\bar E)\), which contains \(F_0\) since \(n\ge2\).
Injectivity of this edge map therefore forces \(H_n(K)=0\), a
contradiction.  All homotopy groups of \(K\) vanish.

The exact homotopy sequence makes \(\bar g\), and hence the original
\(g\), an isomorphism on every homotopy group.  The complete CW-domain
compression argument in \cref{mapsI:pf:cw-inverses} supplies an actual
inverse \(\bar h:T_X\to S^6\) to \(\bar g\), with both inverse
homotopies.  Set
\[
 h_X=\bar h\beta:X\longrightarrow S^6.
\]
Then \(h_Xg=\bar h\bar g\simeq1_{S^6}\).  For the other composition,
use \(g=\alpha\bar g\), then \(\bar g\bar h\simeq1_{T_X}\), then
the exact equality \(\alpha\beta=1_X\), to obtain
\[
 gh_X=\alpha\bar g\bar h\beta\simeq\alpha\beta=1_X.
\]
Both homotopies concern the original spaces and the original degree-one
map.  The orientation generator in \eqref{mapsI:course:degree-one}
has not been rescaled.
\end{proof}

% END I_paperI_course_homotopy

% BEGIN I_wb_algebraic_dimension
\section{The direct algebraic-reduction proof}
\label{wb:sec:algebraic-dimension}

The calculation in this section is independent of the integral topology of
\(X\).  It uses the period family of
\cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit} and the proper connected fibration of
\cref{wb:thm:candidate-global-geometry}; it does not use \(H^2(X;\mathbb Z)\),
the sphere-recognition argument, or any theorem of
Campana--Demailly--Peternell.

\begin{lemma}[algebraic reduction of a two-dimensional torus]
\label{wb:lem:torus-algebraic-reduction-audit}
Let \(T\) be a complex torus of dimension two.  Suppose
\[
 \operatorname{NS}(T)=\mathbb Z\eta,\qquad \eta^2\ne0,
\]
and the Appell--Humbert Hermitian form \(H_\eta\) is nondegenerate and
indefinite.  Then \(a(T)=0\).
\end{lemma}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cite[\S8, p.~2437]{PareschiPopaSchnell2017}}


\begin{proof}
The algebraic reduction of a compact complex torus is a quotient
\(q:T\to A=T/K\) by a connected complex subtorus, with \(A\) an abelian
variety and \(\dim A=a(T)\)
\cite[\S8, p.~2437]{PareschiPopaSchnell2017}.

Assume \(a(T)>0\).  If \(a(T)=2\), then \(T\) is an abelian surface.  An
ample line bundle has first Chern class \(n\eta\), \(n\ne0\), and its
Appell--Humbert form \(nH_\eta\) is positive definite.  This contradicts
the indefiniteness of \(H_\eta\).

If \(a(T)=1\), then \(A\) is an elliptic curve.  For a point \(p\in A\),
put
\[
 \varphi=q^*c_1(\mathcal O_A(p))\in\operatorname{NS}(T).
\]
The class is nonzero: for any translation-invariant Kahler form \(\omega\)
on \(T\), the projection formula gives
\(\int_T\varphi\wedge\omega=\int_K\omega>0\).  But
\(\varphi^2=0\), since \(A\) is a curve.  Writing
\(\varphi=n\eta\), \(n\ne0\), yields
\(0=n^2\eta^2\ne0\), a contradiction.  Both possible positive algebraic
dimensions are excluded.
\end{proof}

Let
\[
 V=\mathbb Z\langle\gamma,u,w,\delta\rangle,
 \qquad
 \eta=u\wedge w+6\gamma\wedge\delta.
\]
For an integral two-class \(E\in\bigwedge^2V\), write its coordinates in
the ordered basis
\((\gamma u,\allowbreak\gamma w,\allowbreak\gamma\delta,\allowbreak uw,\allowbreak u\delta,\allowbreak w\delta)\) as
\(E_{\gamma u},\ldots,E_{w\delta}\), and set
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_E={}&E_{\gamma u}-E_{\gamma w}\tau-E_{\gamma\delta}\mu
 +6E_{uw}\mu+E_{u\delta}\beta\\
&+E_{w\delta}(6\mu^2-\tau\beta).
\end{aligned}
\tag{AD.1}
\]

\begin{proposition}[very general Neron--Severi group]
\label{wb:prop:very-general-torus-audit}
\ For the descended period family of
\cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit}, outside a countable subset of
\(B^\circ\) the smooth fibre
\(F_b\) satisfies
\[
 \operatorname{NS}(F_b)=\mathbb Z\eta,
 \qquad a(F_b)=0.
\tag{AD.2}
\]
\end{proposition}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit}; \cref{wb:thm:coinvariants}; \cref{wb:lem:torus-algebraic-reduction-audit}}


\begin{proof}
The two holomorphic one-forms defining the Hodge subspace are
\[
 \sigma_1=6\mu\gamma+\tau u+w,
 \qquad
 \sigma_2=\beta\gamma+\mu u+\delta.
\]
The determinant inequality (2.2) gives
\(V_{\mathbb C}=F^1\oplus\overline{F^1}\), where
\(F^1=\langle\sigma_1,\sigma_2\rangle\).  For a real two-class \(E\),
the Hodge decomposition therefore gives
\[
 E\in H^{1,1}(F_b)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 E\wedge\sigma_1\wedge\sigma_2=0.
\]
Expanding the wedge product gives
\[
 E\wedge\sigma_1\wedge\sigma_2
 =P_E\,\gamma\wedge u\wedge w\wedge\delta.
\tag{AD.3}
\]

We next determine exactly which \(P_E\) vanish identically.  Suppose
\[
 a+b\tau+c\mu+d\beta+e(6\mu^2-\tau\beta)\equiv0.
\tag{AD.4}
\]
Apply the cusp transformation
\((\tau,\mu,\beta)\mapsto(\tau-1,\mu,\beta+1)\) and subtract.  This gives
\[
 -b+d+e(\beta-\tau+1)=0.
\]
Because \(\beta-\tau\) is translated by two, \(e=0\), and then \(d=b\).
Apply the order-four transformation in (2.1), subtract (AD.4), and multiply
by \(-\tau\).  One obtains
\[
 6b\mu^2+c(\tau-1)\mu+b(\tau^2+3\tau+1)-c\tau=0.
\]
Subtract its cusp translate:
\[
 c\mu+2b(\tau+1)-c=0.
\tag{AD.5}
\]
Translate (AD.5) once around the cusp.  Since \(\mu\) is invariant and
\(\tau\mapsto\tau-1\), subtracting the translated identity from (AD.5)
gives \(2b=0\).  Thus \(b=0\), and (AD.5) becomes
\(c(\mu-1)=0\).  If \(c\ne0\), then \(\mu\equiv1\), whereas the
order-four law would give
\(1=\mu\circ g_2=1+1/\tau\), an impossibility.  Hence \(c=0\), then
\(b=d=0\), and finally \(a=0\).
Thus the five functions
\[
 1,\quad\tau,\quad\mu,\quad\beta,\quad6\mu^2-\tau\beta
\]
are linearly independent over \(\mathbb C\).

Reading the coefficients in (AD.1) now gives
\[
 P_E\equiv0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad E\in\mathbb Z\eta.
\tag{AD.6}
\]
For each other integral class, the zero set of \(P_E\) on the connected
Riemann surface \(\mathfrak h_z\) is discrete, hence countable.  There are
only countably many integral classes.  The class
\(\eta=q=uw+6\gamma\delta\) is monodromy invariant by
\cref{wb:thm:coinvariants}, so it defines a class on every marked fibre after
descent.  The image in \(B^\circ\) of the countable union of the remaining
discrete zero sets is still countable.  A base point outside that image has
no additional integral \((1,1)\)-class on any lift, proving the
Neron--Severi statement on the quotient family.

Finally,
\[
 \eta^2=12\,\gamma\wedge u\wedge w\wedge\delta.
\tag{AD.7}
\]
For a nondegenerate alternating form \(E\), write \(E^\vee\) for its
inverse alternating form on the dual real vector space.  If
\(G_\eta=(i\eta^\vee(\sigma_a,\overline{\sigma_b}))_{a,b}\), direct
inversion of the alternating-form matrix and substitution give
\[
G_\eta=
\begin{pmatrix}
2\operatorname{Im}\tau&2\operatorname{Im}\mu\\
2\operatorname{Im}\mu&\frac13\operatorname{Im}\beta
\end{pmatrix},
\]
\[
\det G_\eta=
\frac23\operatorname{Im}\tau
\left(\operatorname{Im}\beta-
\frac{6(\operatorname{Im}\mu)^2}{\operatorname{Im}\tau}\right)<0.
\tag{AD.8}
\]
Here is the Appell--Humbert bridge needed to read the inertia of this
matrix.  With the convention \(E=\operatorname{Im}H_E\), one has
\[
 E=\frac1{2i}\sum_{a,b}(H_E)_{ab}\,
       \sigma_a\wedge\overline{\sigma_b}.
\]
Thus, in the ordered basis
\((\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\overline{\sigma_1},\overline{\sigma_2})\), the
upper-right block of the alternating-form matrix of \(E\) is
\(A=-(i/2)H_E\).  Inverting the block matrix gives
\[
 E^\vee(\sigma_a,\overline{\sigma_b})
   =[-(A^t)^{-1}]_{ab}
   =-2i(\overline{H_E}^{\,-1})_{ab},
 \qquad
 G_E=2\overline{H_E}^{\,-1}.
\tag{3.8a}
\]
The displayed \(G_\eta\) is real symmetric, so
\(H_\eta=2G_\eta^{-1}\).  Inversion and multiplication by a positive scalar
preserve inertia.  Hence \(H_\eta\) is nondegenerate and indefinite, while
(AD.7) is nonzero.
Apply \cref{wb:lem:torus-algebraic-reduction-audit}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[meromorphic descent]
\label{wb:lem:meromorphic-descent-audit}
Let \(f:X\to B\) be a proper surjective holomorphic map from a connected
complex threefold to a connected compact Riemann surface, with connected
fibres, and a submersion over
\(B^\circ=B\setminus\Sigma\), where \(\Sigma\) is finite and
\(B^\circ\ne\varnothing\).  If
\(g\in\mathcal M(X)\) is constant on the fibres over an uncountable subset
of \(B^\circ\), then there is a unique \(\varphi\in\mathcal M(B)\) such that
\(g=f^*\varphi\).
\end{lemma}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; the explicit constructions and calculations in the proof}


\begin{proof}
Let \(P\) be the polar divisor of \(g\), and put
\(\Omega=f^{-1}(B^\circ)\setminus|P|\).  A proper analytic subset of a
connected complex manifold has real codimension at least two and does not
disconnect it.  First note that \(f^{-1}(B^\circ)\) is connected.  Indeed,
each of its connected components is open, and its image is open because
\(f\) is a submersion and closed because the base change
\(f^{-1}(B^\circ)\to B^\circ\) is proper.  Since \(B^\circ\) is connected,
every component would meet every fibre; connectedness of the fibres
therefore permits only one component.  Removing \(|P|\) now leaves
\(\Omega\) connected.  Only finitely many fibres are
components of \(|P|\).  For every other \(b\), the complement
\(F_b\cap\Omega\) of a proper analytic subset in the connected manifold
\(F_b\) is connected.

On \(\Omega\), define the analytic set
\[
 Z=\{dg\wedge f^*(dt)=0\},
\]
where \(t\) is any local coordinate on \(B\).  If \(g|_{F_b}\) is
constant, then \(F_b\cap\Omega\subset Z\).  If \(Z\ne\Omega\), then, because
\(\Omega\) is second countable, \(Z\) has at most countably many
irreducible components.  Each irreducible two-dimensional fibre contained
in \(Z\) is one of those components, and distinct fibres give distinct
components.  This contradicts the uncountable hypothesis.  Therefore
\(Z=\Omega\).

It follows that \(dg\) annihilates \(\ker df\).  Connectedness of
\(F_b\cap\Omega\), together with local holomorphic sections of the
submersion, gives \(g=\varphi\circ f\) on \(\Omega\), for a holomorphic
\(\varphi\) away from finitely many points of \(B\).

Fix such a point \(t_0\).  Choose a general holomorphic curve germ
\(\kappa:(\Delta,0)\to(X,x)\), not contained in \(|P|\), with
\[
 f\circ\kappa(s)=t_0+s^ku(s),\qquad u(0)\ne0.
\]
If \(g\circ\kappa\) has pole order at most \(M\), then
\(|g\circ\kappa(s)|\le C|s|^{-M}\).  After shrinking the disc, boundedness
above and below of \(|u|\) gives constants \(c,C_1>0\) such that
\[
 c|t-t_0|^{1/k}\le |s|\le C_1|t-t_0|^{1/k}
\]
on each local inverse branch.  Therefore
\[
 |\varphi(t)|\le C_2|t-t_0|^{-M/k}
\]
away from the image of a discrete exceptional set, and then everywhere on
the punctured disc by holomorphy.  For any integer \(N>M/k\), the function
\((t-t_0)^N\varphi(t)\) is bounded and extends holomorphically.  Thus
\(\varphi\) is meromorphic at \(t_0\).  Repeating at the finitely many
exceptional points produces \(\varphi\in\mathcal M(B)\).  Equality on the
dense open set \(\Omega\) gives equality of meromorphic functions on \(X\),
and surjectivity of \(f\) gives uniqueness.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[algebraic dimension and algebraic reduction]
\label{wb:thm:algebraic-dimension-audit}
\ For the global holomorphic family of
\cref{wb:thm:candidate-global-geometry},
\[
 \mathcal M(X)=f^*\mathcal M(\mathbb P^1)=f^*\mathbb C(t),
 \qquad a(X)=1,
\tag{AD.9}
\]
and \(f\) is the algebraic reduction.
\end{theorem}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{wb:thm:candidate-global-geometry}; \cref{wb:prop:very-general-torus-audit}; \cref{wb:lem:meromorphic-descent-audit}}


\begin{proof}
By \cref{wb:prop:very-general-torus-audit}, all but countably many smooth
fibres have algebraic dimension zero.  Let \(g\in\mathcal M(X)\).  Only
finitely many fibres are components of its polar divisor, so on uncountably
many of the preceding fibres the restriction of \(g\) is a meromorphic
function on a torus of algebraic dimension zero and is therefore constant.
By \cref{wb:lem:meromorphic-descent-audit}, \(g=f^*\varphi\) for a unique
\(\varphi\in\mathcal M(\mathbb P^1)\).  The reverse inclusion is immediate,
and (AD.9) follows.  Since \(f\) is proper, surjective, has connected fibres,
and induces the equality of meromorphic function fields, it is the algebraic
reduction.
\end{proof}


% END I_wb_algebraic_dimension

% BEGIN I_cdp_monodromy_proof
\section{Integral monodromy: the kernel calculation}\label{app:cdp-monodromy}
We retain the complete kernel calculation for Theorem~\ref{fam:st:F.1.1}.
\begin{proof}
\textit{Step 1: the integral stabilizer.}
Since $Ge=e$ and $G$ preserves $\Omega$, the identity
$\Omega(Gv,e)=\Omega(v,e)$ forces the first row of $G$ to be
$(1,0,0,0)$. The last column is $e$, so write
\[
 G=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0\\v&B&0\\t&w&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Preservation of $\Omega$ is equivalent to
$B^tJB=J$ and $6w+v^tJB=0$. The first equality gives
$B\in\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. The second and integrality of $w$
give $v^tJB\in6\mathbb Z^2$. Because $JB$ is unimodular,
$v=6x$ for a unique integral vector $x$. This proves the asserted
parametrization, including its converse. Block multiplication gives
\begin{equation}\label{cdp:eq:parabolic-law}
 g(B,x,t)g(C,y,s)=g(BC,x+By,t+s-6x^tJBy).
\end{equation}

\textit{Step 2: the cyclic character of the middle block.}
Put
\[
 S=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 a=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&-1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
 T=Sa=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The Euclidean algorithm on the first column of an integral
unimodular matrix shows that $S,T$, hence $a,S$, generate
$\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. Their images in
$\operatorname{PSL}_2(\mathbb Z)$ have orders three and two.
For the fractional-linear action on $\mathbb R\cup\{\infty\}$,
$a$ sends $(0,\infty)$ into $(-1,0)$, $a^2$ sends
$(0,\infty)$ into $(-\infty,-1)$, and $S$ sends
$(-\infty,0)$ into $(0,\infty)$. The reduced-word ping-pong argument
therefore identifies the subgroup they generate in the projective
group with the free product of their cyclic subgroups: a reduced
alternating word, after conjugation to start and end in the
order-three factor, sends the positive interval into the negative
interval and cannot be the identity. Such a conjugation is possible
for every nontrivial cyclically reduced alternating word because
the order-three factor has two nonidentity elements; a word in one
factor is already nonidentity. Lifting to the integral group gives
\[
 \operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)
 =\langle a,S\mid a^3=S^4=1,\ [a,S^2]=1\rangle.
\]
Indeed, the presented group maps surjectively onto the integral
group; quotienting its central element $S^2$ gives the just-proved
free product, and $S^2$ maps to $-I$, so the map has trivial kernel.
The assignments $\alpha(a)=4$ and $\alpha(S)=9$ respect these
relations modulo $12$ and give $\alpha(T)=1$. They define the
required homomorphism, which is unique because $S,T$ generate.

\textit{Step 3: the character of the stabilizer.}
Modulo two, $Q$ vanishes exactly at the origin of $(\mathbb Z/2)^2$.
Consequently $Q(Bx)=Q(x)$ modulo two for every integral unimodular
$B$. Also
\[
 Q(x+y)-Q(x)-Q(y)=x_1y_2+x_2y_1=x^tJy\pmod2.
\]
Together with \eqref{cdp:eq:parabolic-law} these identities show that
\[
 \chi(g(B,x,t))=t+6Q(x)-\alpha(B)\pmod {12}
\]
is a homomorphism. It is surjective because
$\chi(g(I,0,1))=1$. Direct substitution gives
\[
 A_1=g(a,(1,-1)^t,-2),\qquad A_2=g(S,(0,-1)^t,3),
 \qquad \chi(A_1)=\chi(A_2)=0.
\]
Thus $\langle A_1,A_2\rangle\subseteq\ker\chi$.

\textit{Step 4: equality with the kernel.}
With $[G,H]=GHG^{-1}H^{-1}$, multiplication in
\eqref{cdp:eq:parabolic-law} gives
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 K&=[A_1,A_2^2]=g(I,(0,-1)^t,6),\\
 U&=A_2KA_2^{-1}=g(I,(1,0)^t,-6),\\
 V&=K^{-1}=g(I,(0,1)^t,-6),\\
 Z&=I+12e\gamma=g(I,0,12),\qquad [U,V]=Z^{-1}.
 \end{aligned}
\]
In particular $U,V,Z$ belong to $\langle A_1,A_2\rangle$. For all
integers $r,s,n$, the multiplication law gives
\[
 U^rV^sZ^n=g(I,(r,s)^t,-6(r+s+rs)+12n).
\]
These are precisely the elements of $\ker\chi$ whose middle block
is $I$. The middle blocks $a,S$ of $A_1,A_2$ generate
$\operatorname{SL}_2(\mathbb Z)$. Given any $G\in\ker\chi$, choose
$H\in\langle A_1,A_2\rangle$ with the same middle block as $G$.
Then $H^{-1}G$ belongs to the already computed kernel over $I$ and
hence to $\langle A_1,A_2\rangle$. Therefore
$\ker\chi=\langle A_1,A_2\rangle$, and surjectivity of $\chi$ proves
the index formula.
\end{proof}

% END I_cdp_monodromy_proof

% BEGIN I_cdp_kuranishi_proof
\section{A second root-bundle derivation of the Kuranishi statement}\label{app:cdp-kuranishi}
We re-derive Theorem~\ref{fam:st:A.5.2}, credited to \citet[Theorem~6.12 and Proposition~6.16]{DuEtAl2026v1}.
\begin{proof}
We confirm the particular implication used here from the root-bundle and cusp-normalization data proved above. On $\mathfrak B=\mathbb P(3,4)$, both vertical and
structure-cohomology bundles are $E=G=\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(-1)$.
The vertical subline is generated by the invariant translation
field; its quotient has twelfth power $\mathcal O(-p_0)$ by the
discriminant's simple cusp zero, hence is $\mathcal O(-1)$ in the
torsion-free root Picard group. The extension splits because
$H^1(\mathcal O(1))=0$. For $G$, relative duality and the
normalization complex of the hexagon give
$\det G=R^2\bar f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O(-1)$; the invariant
integral cocycle $\gamma$ is nonzero on every ordinary fibre and
on the dual-graph cycle at the cusp. It gives the same split
extension. This checks the nonvanishing at the cusp required by the structure-sheaf calculation.

The horizontal logarithmic line is $\mathcal O(-5)$. Projection
and Leray applied to
$0\to\bar f^*E\to T_X(-\log W)\to\bar f^*\mathcal O(-5)\to0$
give logarithmic tangent cohomology $(1,1,0,0)$: every nontrivial
root line appearing is one of
$\mathcal O(-1),\mathcal O(-2),\mathcal O(-5),\mathcal O(-6)$,
whose coarse direct image is $\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1)$,
while the two surviving trivial summands lie in degrees zero
and one. The branch-normal sequence has quotient
$\eta_*K_{\mathrm dP_6}$, with cohomology $(0,0,1)$; the local
map sends each ambient vector field to its separate normal
coefficient on each branch. Hence its exact cohomology sequence
gives $(1,1,1,0)$ for $T_X$.

The parameter derivative is nonzero. The fixed real marking of
the torus lattice gives the constant Beltrami class
\[
 -\frac{1}{2iD}\,\partial_{\zeta_2}\otimes
 (d\bar\zeta_2-a\,d\bar\zeta_1),
 \quad a=\frac{\operatorname{Im}\mu}{\operatorname{Im}\tau},
 \quad D=\operatorname{Im}\beta_c
       -\frac{6(\operatorname{Im}\mu)^2}{\operatorname{Im}\tau}.
\]
A nonzero constant Dolbeault tensor on a torus is not exact,
because integration of every derivative of a periodic coefficient
is zero. A first-order trivialization of $X_c$ would preserve
the relative complete pencil $|-2K|$. Its induced infinitesimal
automorphism of $\mathbb P^1$ fixes all three critical values:
the equations $t=s^3$, $t-1=s^4$, and $q=xyz$ make each critical
value a constant section over the dual numbers. An infinitesimal
projective transformation fixing three distinct points is zero.
The trivialization would therefore trivialize the nonzero fibre
class just displayed, a contradiction. Thus the period derivative
spans the one-dimensional $H^1(T_X)$.

Write the Kuranishi local algebra as $\mathbb C\{z\}/I$ in its
one-dimensional tangent space. The existing proper period family
defines a local classifying map $z\mapsto\phi(s)$ with
$\phi'(0)\ne0$. The analytic inverse-function theorem makes
$\mathbb C\{z\}\to\mathbb C\{s\}$ an isomorphism. Since it
annihilates $I$, necessarily $I=0$. This verifies smoothness and
reducedness as well as miniversality, and every sufficiently small
deformation is a member of that period family.
\end{proof}
% END I_cdp_kuranishi_proof

% BEGIN I_paperI_hodge_line
\subsection{The relative Hodge line}
Put $e=d\zeta_1\wedge d\zeta_2$ on the marked torus family.
Retain the negative-phase coordinates $s_j\circ g_j=\zeta_js_j$,
with $(m_1,m_2)=(3,4)$, $\zeta_j=e^{-2\pi i/m_j}$,
$t_j=s_j^{m_j}$, and $f^{-1}(p_j)=m_jS_j$.
\begin{lemma}[determinant characters and the Hodge line]
\label{mapsI:hodge:line}\label{wb:lem:hodge-line-audit}
\ Let
\[
 \mathfrak K=f_*\omega_{X/B}.
\]
Then \(\mathfrak K\) is invertible and
\[
 \mathfrak K\simeq\mathcal O_B(1).
\tag{HL.9.1}
\]
More precisely,
\[
 \det R_{g_1}=-\frac1\tau,\qquad
 \det R_{g_2}=\frac1\tau,\qquad
 \det R_{g_0}=1,
\tag{HL.9.2}
\]
and at the fixed points
\[
 \det R_{g_j}(z_j)=\zeta_j^{a_j},
 \qquad (a_1,a_2)=(2,1).
\tag{HL.9.3}
\]
The form \(e\) generates \(\mathfrak K\) at the cusp, while a unit times
\(s_j^{-a_j}e\) generates it at \(p_j\).
\end{lemma}
\Uses{the hypotheses, notation and definitions stated here; \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit}; \cref{wb:prop:candidate-finite-fillings}; \cite[Chapter~VII, Theorems~3--4 and Proposition~8]{Serre1973}}


The Hodge line and finite determinant characters
are known from \citet[Lemma~9.10 and Proposition~9.11, pp.~70--71]{AC2026}.
The complete modular-frame and root-character re-derivation follows.


\begin{proof}
The period equivariance in \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit} gives
\[
 R_g(z)\Pi(z)\lambda=\Pi(gz)A_g\lambda.
\]
Using
\[
 A_1\widehat w=\widehat u-\widehat w,\quad
 A_1\widehat\delta=\widehat\delta,\qquad
 A_2\widehat w=-\widehat u+\widehat\delta,\quad
 A_2\widehat\delta=\widehat\delta,
\]
and writing \(\tau^\sharp=\tau(g_jz)\),
\(\mu^\sharp=\mu(g_jz)\), direct multiplication gives
\[
 R_{g_1}=
 \begin{pmatrix}\tau^\sharp-1&0\\ \mu^\sharp&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad
 R_{g_2}=
 \begin{pmatrix}-\tau^\sharp&0\\1-\mu^\sharp&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
The transformation laws
\(\tau\circ g_1=(\tau-1)/\tau\) and
\(\tau\circ g_2=-1/\tau\) prove (HL.9.2) at \(g_1,g_2\); the cusp formulas
give \(R_{g_0}=I\).  Since \(\widehat\delta\) is fixed, one eigenvalue is
\(1\).  At \(\tau(z_1)=\rho=e^{\pi i/3}\), the other is
\(\rho-1=e^{2\pi i/3}=\zeta_1^2\); at \(\tau(z_2)=i\), it is
\(-i=\zeta_2\).  This proves (HL.9.3).

We determine the extension over a finite filling without suppressing the
ramification.  On \(J'_j\), the nowhere-zero form \(ds_j\wedge e\)
transforms by
\[
 (\widetilde g_j^{\log})^*(ds_j\wedge e)
 =\chi_j(s_j)\,ds_j\wedge e,
 \qquad \chi_j=\zeta_j\det R_{g_j}.
\tag{HL.9.4}
\]
Iteration \(m_j\) times shows
\(\prod_{r=0}^{m_j-1}\chi_j(\zeta_j^rs)=1\).
Write \(\chi_j(s)=\chi_j(0)e^{\psi(s)}\), with \(\psi(0)=0\).
The product identity says that the power series of \(\psi\) has no terms
whose degree is divisible by \(m_j\).  Hence
\[
 \varphi(s)-\varphi(\zeta_js)=\psi(s)
\]
has a holomorphic solution, obtained coefficientwise by division by
\(1-\zeta_j^n\).  Therefore
\[
 s^{k_j}e^{\varphi(s)}ds\wedge e,
 \qquad k_j=m_j-1-a_j,
\tag{HL.9.5}
\]
is invariant: \(\chi_j(0)=\zeta_j^{1+a_j}\), so invariance is equivalent
to \(k_j+1+a_j\equiv0\pmod {m_j}\).  We now distinguish the descended
canonical section from the generator of its direct image.  Let
\[
 q_j:J'_j\longrightarrow N_j,\qquad
 \widetilde f_j:J'_j\longrightarrow\Delta_j,\qquad
 \varpi_j:\Delta_j\longrightarrow D_j
\]
denote the finite quotient, the torus-family projection, and the cyclic base
quotient, respectively, so that
\[
 f_j\circ q_j=\varpi_j\circ\widetilde f_j,
 \qquad t_j=s_j^{m_j}.
\]
Put \(\mathcal A_j=\widetilde f_j^{-1}(0)=\{s_j=0\}\) and
\(G_j=\langle\widetilde g_j^{\log}\rangle\).  The action is free by
\cref{wb:prop:candidate-finite-fillings}; hence \(q_j\) is finite \'etale
and \(q_j^{-1}(S_j)=\mathcal A_j\).

The invariant form in (HL.9.5), now denoted
\[
 \sigma_j=s_j^{k_j}e^{\varphi(s_j)}ds_j\wedge e,
 \qquad k_j=m_j-1-a_j,
\tag{HL.9.5a}
\]
descends uniquely to
\(\overline\sigma_j\in H^0(N_j,K_{N_j})\) with
\(q_j^*\overline\sigma_j=\sigma_j\).  Since \(e^{\varphi(s_j)}\) is a
unit and \(ds_j\wedge e\) is nowhere vanishing,
\[
 \operatorname{div}_{J'_j}(\sigma_j)=k_j\mathcal A_j.
\]
Because \(q_j\) is \'etale,
\[
 q_j^*\operatorname{div}_{N_j}(\overline\sigma_j)
 =\operatorname{div}_{J'_j}(q_j^*\overline\sigma_j)
 =k_j\mathcal A_j=q_j^*(k_jS_j).
\]
Faithfulness of finite surjective pullback on Cartier divisors therefore gives
\[
 \operatorname{div}_{N_j}(\overline\sigma_j)=k_jS_j.
\tag{HL.9.5b}
\]
Thus (HL.9.5a) is a canonical section with that divisor, not a nowhere-vanishing
frame when \(k_j>0\); explicitly, \(k_1=0\) and \(k_2=2\).

For the direct-image generator, let
\[
 \vartheta_j=(ds_j\wedge e)\otimes(dt_j)^{-1}
\tag{HL.9.5c}
\]
be the nowhere-vanishing frame of
\[
 q_j^*\omega_{N_j/D_j}
 =K_{J'_j}\otimes(f_j\circ q_j)^*K_{D_j}^{-1}.
\]
Here \((dt_j)^{-1}\) is the pulled-back frame of the inverse canonical line
of \(D_j\), not division by the differential of \(s_j^{m_j}\).  Put
\(\vartheta'_j=e^{\varphi(s_j)}\vartheta_j\).  The defining equation for
\(\varphi\), together with
\(\chi_j(s)=\chi_j(0)e^{\psi(s)}\) and
\(\chi_j(0)=\zeta_j^{1+a_j}\), gives
\[
 (\widetilde g_j^{\log})^*\vartheta'_j
 =\zeta_j^{1+a_j}\vartheta'_j.
\tag{HL.9.5d}
\]
Every holomorphic coefficient of a relative top form is pulled back from
\(\Delta_j\), because the fibres of \(\widetilde f_j\) are connected compact
complex tori.  Hence
\[
 \widetilde f_{j*}q_j^*\omega_{N_j/D_j}
 =\mathcal O_{\Delta_j}\vartheta'_j.
\]
For \(F(s_j)\in\mathcal O_{\Delta_j}\), the section
\(F(s_j)\vartheta'_j\) is \(G_j\)-invariant exactly when
\[
 F(\zeta_js_j)\zeta_j^{1+a_j}=F(s_j).
\tag{HL.9.5e}
\]
Writing \(F(s_j)=\sum_{n\ge0}c_ns_j^n\), this says that \(c_n=0\) unless
\[
 n+1+a_j\equiv0\pmod {m_j},
 \qquad\text{equivalently}\qquad n\equiv k_j\pmod {m_j}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \left((\varpi_j)_*\widetilde f_{j*}
 q_j^*\omega_{N_j/D_j}\right)^{G_j}
 =\mathcal O_{D_j}\cdot s_j^{k_j}\vartheta'_j,
\]
and finite descent gives the precise invariant-module identity
\[
 f_{j*}\omega_{N_j/D_j}
 =\mathcal O_{D_j}\cdot s_j^{k_j}\vartheta'_j.
\tag{HL.9.5f}
\]
Finally, over \(\Delta_j^*\), the differential identity
\[
 dt_j=m_js_j^{m_j-1}ds_j
\]
identifies this generator with
\[
 s_j^{k_j}\vartheta'_j
 =\frac{e^{\varphi(s_j)}}{m_j}
 s_j^{k_j-(m_j-1)}e
 =\frac{e^{\varphi(s_j)}}{m_j}s_j^{-a_j}e.
\tag{HL.9.5g}
\]
Thus a unit times \(s_j^{-a_j}e\) generates
\(f_{j*}\omega_{N_j/D_j}=(f_*\omega_{X/B})|_{D_j}\), whereas the
canonical section (HL.9.5a) itself has divisor \(k_jS_j\).

At the cusp, in every smooth toric chart the unimodular monomial change of
coordinates turns
\[
 \Omega_0=\frac{dx_1}{x_1}\wedge
          \frac{dx_2}{x_2}\wedge dt_c
\]
into a unit times the ordinary coordinate volume form.  Thus it generates
the canonical line.  It is invariant under translations and under the
unimodular shears defining the quotient.  Under the punctured-overlap map,
\(\Omega_0=(2\pi i)^2dt_c\wedge e\), so \(e\) generates
\(\mathfrak K\) at \(p_0\).

It remains to compute the degree.  The modular-form calculation already
used in the proof of \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit} gives
\[
 \Theta=
 \left(\frac{E_4^2E_6^{1/2}}{\Delta_{\rm mod}}\right)\!\circ\tau.
\]
The square root exists because the zeros of \(E_6\circ\tau\) have even
order.  The classical modular weights are $4,6,12$
\cite[Chapter~VII, Theorems~3--4 and Proposition~8]{Serre1973}.
Thus the squares of the automorphy factors of $\Theta$ and $e$ agree.
Their quotient is a constant sign for each generator. At $z_1$, the
zero of $\Theta$ has order two, so its factor has limiting value
$\zeta_1^2=-1/\rho=\det R_{g_1}(z_1)$. At $z_2$, its zero has order
one, so that limit is $\zeta_2=-i=1/i=\det R_{g_2}(z_2)$.
These limits fix both signs. At the cusp the normalized Fourier
expansions give a single-valued square root with nonzero constant
term, hence factor one under $\tau\mapsto\tau-1$.
Consequently $\Theta$ has exactly the automorphy factor of $e$.  The orders are
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_{z_1}\Theta=2=a_1,\qquad
 \operatorname{ord}_{z_2}\Theta=1=a_2,\qquad
 \Theta=t_c^{-1}\cdot(\text{unit})
\tag{HL.9.6}
\]
at the cusp.  Consequently \(\mathsf e=\Theta^{-1}e\) is single-valued.
At \(p_j\) it is a unit times \(s_j^{-a_j}e\); at \(p_0\) it is a unit
times \(t_ce\).  Hence it is a global section of \(\mathfrak K\) with the
single simple zero \(p_0\).  This proves
\(\mathfrak K\simeq\mathcal O_B(p_0)\simeq\mathcal O_B(1)\).
Finally, \(\mathfrak K\) is torsion free of generic rank one on the smooth
curve \(B\), hence is invertible.
\end{proof}

% END I_paperI_hodge_line

% BEGIN I_working_analytic_picard_proofs
\section{Independent normalization and analytic Picard proofs}\label{inv:wb:analytic-picard-proofs}
\subsection{The cusp structure sheaf}

\subsubsection{structure-sheaf cohomology of the cusp fibre}\label{inv:wbproof:lem:cusp-structure-sheaf-audit}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:A1.0}.


\begin{proof}
Let \(D_1,D_2,D_3\simeq\mathbb P^1\) be the double curves and \(P,Q\) the
two triple points, with the branch order fixed in the proof of
\cref{mapsI:top:thm:p0-integral-specialization}.  The normalization complex is
\[
0\longrightarrow\mathcal O_W\longrightarrow
 \nu_*\mathcal O_{\mathrm{dP}_6}\xrightarrow{\delta_0}
 \bigoplus_{k=1}^3\mathcal O_{D_k}\xrightarrow{\delta_1}
 \mathbb C_P\oplus\mathbb C_Q\longrightarrow0,
\tag{WBA.9.10}\label{inv:wb:eq:9.10}
\]
where \(\delta_0\) is the difference of the two branch restrictions and
\[
 \delta_1(g_1,g_2,g_3)
 =(g_1(P)-g_2(P)+g_3(P),
   g_1(Q)-g_2(Q)+g_3(Q)).
\]
For completeness, exactness is stalkwise.  At a generic double point it is
the fibre-product sequence
\[
0\to\mathbb C\{x,y,z\}/(xy)
 \to\mathbb C\{y,z\}\oplus\mathbb C\{x,z\}
 \to\mathbb C\{z\}\to0.
\]
At a triple point it is the augmented branch complex for
\(\mathbb C\{x,y,z\}/(xyz)\): three branch rings, three pairwise
intersection rings, and the common residue field, with alternating
differences.  The augmented two-simplex complex is exact; successively
lifting compatible power series proves exactness of the analytic rings.
Away from the singular locus the first arrow is an isomorphism.

The same formulas give an exact complex with \(\mathbb C\) in place of
\(\mathcal O\).  Since \(\mathrm{dP}_6\) is rational and each \(D_k\) is a
rational curve, the positive structure-sheaf cohomology of every term on
the right of \eqref{inv:wb:eq:9.10} vanishes.  Hypercohomology therefore reduces to
\[
 \mathbb C\xrightarrow{0}\mathbb C^3
 \xrightarrow{d_1}\mathbb C^2,
 \qquad
 d_1(a_1,a_2,a_3)=(s,s),\quad s=a_1-a_2+a_3.
\tag{WBA.9.11}\label{inv:wb:eq:9.11}
\]
Its cohomology has dimensions \(1,2,1\), proving \cref{inv:A1.0}.

For the constant-sheaf complex, the row of degree zero is again \eqref{inv:wb:eq:9.11},
the row of degree one vanishes, and the remaining degree-two row begins
with \(H^2(\mathrm{dP}_6;\mathbb C)\).  The comparison induced by
\(\mathbb C_W\hookrightarrow\mathcal O_W\) is the identity on \eqref{inv:wb:eq:9.11} and
zero on the positive rows of the target.  It follows that the degree-one comparison of \cref{inv:A1.0} is an
isomorphism, while in degree two it maps the dual-complex summand
\(\ker\nu^*\) isomorphically onto \(H^2(W,\mathcal O_W)\).

Choose the basis \(\gamma_W,u_W\in H^1(W;\mathbb Z)\) whose intrinsic
specializations are \(\gamma,u\), respectively; it exists and is unique by
\cref{mapsI:top:thm:p0-integral-specialization}.  Their cup product is nonzero,
because its specialization is
\(\gamma\wedge u\ne0\in H^2(F;\mathbb Z)\).  Its pullback to
\(\mathrm{dP}_6\) is zero since
\(H^1(\mathrm{dP}_6;\mathbb C)=0\).  The degree-two comparison therefore
sends it to a nonzero element of \(H^2(W,\mathcal O_W)\).  The images of
\(\gamma_W,u_W\) form a basis by the degree-one comparison of \cref{inv:A1.0}, and both sides of the cup-product assertion of \cref{inv:A1.0} are
one-dimensional.  Hence the cup-product assertion of \cref{inv:A1.0} is an isomorphism.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Direct images, base change, and the Picard line}

\subsubsection{structure-sheaf direct images}\label{inv:wbproof:thm:structure-direct-images-audit}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:A1.0}.


\begin{proof}
The proper map has connected fibres and \(B\) is normal, so Stein
factorization gives \(f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O_B\).

The map is flat.  A local parameter on \(B\) pulls back to a nonzero
element of the regular local domain \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\); if it vanished
identically near one point, analytic continuation on the connected
manifold would make \(f\) constant.  Thus \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\) is
torsion-free, hence flat, over the discrete valuation ring
\(\mathcal O_{B,f(x)}\).

Over \(B^\circ\), the fibres are two-dimensional complex tori and their
structure-sheaf cohomology dimensions are \(1,2,1\).  At the cusp the same
dimensions hold by \cref{wb:lem:cusp-structure-sheaf-audit}.  Grauert's
theorem therefore gives local freeness of ranks \(1,2,1\) and base change
on a neighbourhood of \(B^\circ\cup\{p_0\}\); the precise analytic statement is
\cite[Chapter~III, \S4, Theorem~4.12]{BS76}, originally due to
Grauert \cite{Grauert1960D}.

At \(p_j\), use the finite cover \(J'_j\to N_j\).  If
\(\widetilde f:J'_j\to\Delta_j\) is the smooth torus family and
\(\pi(s)=s^{m_j}\), exactness of finite-group invariants in characteristic
zero gives
\[
 R^qf_*\mathcal O_{N_j}
 =\bigl(\pi_*R^q\widetilde f_*\mathcal O_{J'_j}\bigr)^{G_j}.
\tag{WBA.9.14}\label{inv:wb:eq:9.14}
\]
After averaging, a free eigenframe \(v\) may be chosen for each character
\(\nu\).  The invariant sections are exactly
\(s^rv\,\mathcal O_{D_j}\), where \(0\le r<m_j\) is determined by
\(\nu\zeta_j^r=1\).  Hence \eqref{inv:wb:eq:9.14} is free of ranks \(1,2,1\).
Higher direct images vanish by the fibre-dimension bound, so these are all
the nonzero direct images.  Since all direct images are locally free, the analytic
cohomology-and-base-change theorem, applied by descending induction from
\(q=2\), proves the base-change assertion of \cref{inv:A1.0} at the finite fibres as well.  In the notation of
\cite[Chapter~III, \S3, Theorem~3.4, Corollaries~3.5, 3.7, and 3.10]
  {BS76}.  Corollary~3.10 says that, for each fixed \(q\),
  freeness of \(R^p f_*\mathcal O_X\) for every \(p\ge q\) is equivalent to
  cohomological flatness in all dimensions \(p\ge q\).  Applying this
  successively with \(q=2,1,0\) gives the displayed base-change maps in every
  relevant degree.  This is a local statement on the base and so applies
  equally to the nonreduced scheme-theoretic fibres.

Write \(G=R^1f_*\mathcal O_X\).  We construct its distinguished section
without using a cellular collapse.  On \(B^\circ\), the monodromy-invariant
integral class \(\gamma\) maps to a holomorphic section
\(\gamma^{0,1}\) of \(G\).  It is nowhere zero there: if its image in
\(H^{0,1}(F)\) vanished, then
\(\gamma\in H^{1,0}(F)\cap H^1(F;\mathbb R)=0\).  On a finite cover it is
a constant invariant class and remains nonzero at \(s_j=0\), so it
descends across \(p_j\).

At the cusp, let \(j:\Delta^*\hookrightarrow\Delta\).  The natural
specialization morphism
\[
 R^1f_*\mathbb C\longrightarrow
 j_*R^1f_*\mathbb C|_{\Delta^*}
\]
is an isomorphism: away from \(0\) this is tautological, while at \(0\) it
is exactly the isomorphism from \(H^1(W;\mathbb C)\) onto the
\(T_0\)-invariant subspace proved in
\cref{mapsI:top:thm:p0-integral-specialization}.  Hence the invariant classes
\(\gamma,u\) extend as sections of \(R^1f_*\mathbb C\) on the whole disc.
The natural morphism induced by \(\mathbb C\hookrightarrow\mathcal O\),
\[
 R^1f_*\mathbb C\otimes\mathcal O_\Delta
 \longrightarrow G|_\Delta,
\]
sends them at the central point to the two classes in
\(H^1(W,\mathcal O_W)\).  These form a basis by
\cref{wb:lem:cusp-structure-sheaf-audit}.  Thus
\(\gamma^{0,1}\) extends across the cusp and is nowhere zero everywhere.
In particular \(\mathcal O_B\gamma^{0,1}\subset G\) is a line subbundle.

Relative duality applies to the proper flat Gorenstein map \(f\): \(X\) is
smooth, the base is a smooth curve, and \(\omega_{X/B}\) is invertible.
Using \cref{wb:lem:hodge-line-audit}, it gives
\[
 R^2f_*\mathcal O_X\simeq\mathfrak K^\vee
 \simeq\mathcal O_B(-1).
\tag{WBA.9.15}\label{inv:wb:eq:9.15}
\]
The relative theorem is the one of Ramis--Ruget--Verdier
\cite[pp.~261--283]{RRV71}; the absolute singular
dualizing-complex comparison is independently recorded in
\cite[Theorems~1--2 and Proposition~2]{RR70}.

The relative cup product
\[
 \bigwedge^2G\longrightarrow R^2f_*\mathcal O_X
\tag{WBA.9.16}\label{inv:wb:eq:9.16}
\]
is an isomorphism.  It is so on every smooth torus fibre.  At the cusp it
is so by the base-change assertion of \cref{inv:A1.0} and \cref{wb:lem:cusp-structure-sheaf-audit}.  At \(p_j\),
choose on the cover an eigenframe \(v_1,v_2\), with
\(v_1=\gamma^{0,1}\) invariant.  Its invariant exponent is \(r_1=0\).
The action on \(v_1\wedge v_2\) is dual to the Hodge character in (9.3),
so its invariant generator is \(s_j^{a_j}(v_1\wedge v_2)\).
The invariant generator for the second line is consequently
\(s_j^{a_j}v_2\), because \(0<a_j<m_j\).  Wedge product sends
\(v_1\wedge(s_j^{a_j}v_2)\) to exactly the invariant generator of the
right side of \eqref{inv:wb:eq:9.16}, with no wrap modulo \(m_j\).

Consequently
\(\det G\simeq R^2f_*\mathcal O_X\simeq\mathcal O_B(-1)\).  The quotient
of \(G\) by its trivial subbundle is \(\mathcal O_B(-1)\), and the
extension splits because
\[
 \operatorname{Ext}^1(\mathcal O_B(-1),\mathcal O_B)
 =H^1(B,\mathcal O_B(1))=0.
\]
This proves \cref{inv:A1.0} and identifies the trivial summand.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{the Picard parameter and fibrewise restriction}\label{inv:wbproof:cor:picard-line-audit}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:C3.1}.


\begin{proof}
The Leray spectral sequence and \(H^1(B,\mathcal O_B)=0\) identify
\[
 H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)=H^0(B,R^1f_*\mathcal O_X)=\mathbb C
\]
by \cref{wb:thm:structure-direct-images-audit}.  Since the verified integral
topology gives \(H^1(X;\mathbb Z)=H^2(X;\mathbb Z)=0\), the analytic
exponential sequence
\[
0\to\mathbb Z\to\mathcal O_X
 \xrightarrow{u\mapsto e^{2\pi iu}}\mathcal O_X^*\to1
\]
identifies \(H^1(X,\mathcal O_X)\) with \(\operatorname{Pic}(X)\) and
shows that every line bundle is topologically trivial.  Under Leray,
restriction is evaluation of a global section of
\(R^1f_*\mathcal O_X\), followed by base change.  The only global section
is a scalar multiple of the nowhere-zero section \(\gamma^{0,1}\), so
evaluation is injective at every point and has the stated image on a
smooth fibre.
\end{proof}



% END I_working_analytic_picard_proofs

% BEGIN I_working_hodge_frolicher_proofs
\section{Hodge numbers, cotangent direct images, and the Fr\"olicher page}
\label{wb:sec:hodge-frolicher}

The independent period, invariant-lattice, residue, and Riemann--Roch
arguments below prove the shared statements in the main text. The holomorphic
form vanishing is re-derived from \citet[Theorem~9.1(vi) and \S9.5]{AC2026};
the precise source-credit record accompanies the statements.

\subsection{Vanishing of holomorphic forms}

We give the direct period calculation of holomorphic-form vanishing.

\subsubsection{candidate-specific holomorphic-form vanishing}\label{inv:wbproof:prop:workbench-holomorphic-form-vanishing}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:A3.1}.


\begin{proof}
Over the marked cover of the smooth part, write the fibre coordinates as
$\zeta=(\zeta_1,\zeta_2)$ and
\[
 \Pi=[Z\mid I_2],\qquad
 Z=\begin{pmatrix}6\mu&\tau\\ \beta&\mu\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Translation by $\lambda\in\Lambda$ sends
$d\zeta$ to $d\zeta+\dot\Pi\lambda\,dz$.  Compactness of each torus fibre
therefore puts every translation-invariant holomorphic form into one of the
following normal forms:
\begin{align*}
 p=1:&\quad a(z)\,dz+c(z)\cdot d\zeta,
       &c(z)\dot Z(z)&=0,\\
 p=2:&\quad dz\wedge\bigl(b(z)\cdot d\zeta\bigr),\\
 p=3:&\quad c(z)\,dz\wedge d\zeta_1\wedge d\zeta_2.
\end{align*}
Indeed, fibrewise periodic coefficients are constant.  A possible affine
part in a coefficient vanishes after restriction to the real span of the
two constant columns of $\Pi$; in degree two this also kills the putative
$d\zeta_1\wedge d\zeta_2$ term because $\dot\tau$ is nonzero on the smooth
base.

The finite fillings are obtained from smooth torus families by free cyclic
quotients, so the displayed coefficients extend holomorphically across the
two elliptic lifts.  At the cusp use the verified toric charts
$t=w_0w_1w_2$.  Substitution of
\[
 d\zeta_i=(2\pi i)^{-1}dx_i/x_i,
 \qquad ds=(2\pi i)^{-1}dt/t
\]
and restriction successively to the coordinate lines and planes shows that
the coefficients of $d\zeta_i$, $ds$, $ds\wedge d\zeta_i$, and
$ds\wedge d\zeta_1\wedge d\zeta_2$ vanish to order at least one in $t$.
Indeed, on every unimodular monomial chart the triple
$(d\log x_1,d\log x_2,d\log t)$ is a constant invertible linear combination
of the $d\log w_j$.  A coefficient $F(t)$ multiplying a nonzero logarithmic
residue is holomorphic only if its constant term vanishes: restricting to
$w_j=0$ gives that residue as $F(0)$, so $F(t)=tG(t)$.  Invertibility of the
monomial change of basis applies this argument to each displayed
coefficient.
Thus every coefficient used below descends with the asserted regularity at
all three points of the base.

The linear part of a deck transformation has the form
\[
 R_g=\begin{pmatrix}r_g&0\\ *&1\end{pmatrix},
 \qquad \jmath_g:=r_g^{-1}=c_g\tau+d_g,
 \qquad g^*(d\tau)=\jmath_g^{-2}d\tau.
\]
For a one-form, the second component $c_2$ is a holomorphic invariant
function on the base and vanishes at the cusp, hence is zero.  The second
column of $c\dot Z=0$ then gives $c_1\dot\tau=0$, so $c_1=0$.  What remains
is a holomorphic one-form on $\mathbb P^1$, and hence vanishes.

For a two-form, $b_2\,dz$ descends to a holomorphic one-form on
$\mathbb P^1$ and is zero.  The remaining form
$\psi=b_1\,dz$ satisfies $g^*\psi=\jmath_g\psi$.  Consequently
\[
 \psi^{\otimes2}\otimes d\tau
\]
is invariant.  At the order-three and order-four points it descends as a
cubic differential with a pole of order at most two, while the toric cusp
estimate gives a pole of order at most one.  It is therefore a section of
\[
 (\Omega^1_{\mathbb P^1})^{\otimes3}
 (2p_1+2p_2+p_0)\simeq\mathcal O_{\mathbb P^1}(-1),
\]
so it is zero.  Since $\dot\tau$ is nonzero on a dense open set,
$\psi=0$.  The coefficient of a three-form obeys the same weight-one law
and the same argument applies.  Hence all three spaces vanish.
\end{proof}

\subsection{The exact one-parameter Hodge diamond}

\subsubsection{Hodge diamond determined up to one integer}\label{inv:wbproof:thm:parametric-hodge-diamond}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:A3.1}.
Here we write $m=h^{1,2}(X)$.


\begin{proof}
The independently reconstructed structure-sheaf direct images are
\[
 f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O,
 \qquad R^1f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(-1),
 \qquad R^2f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O(-1)
\]
by \cref{wb:thm:structure-direct-images-audit}.  Coherent Leray on
$\mathbb P^1$ therefore gives
\[
 (h^{0,0},h^{0,1},h^{0,2},h^{0,3})=(1,1,0,0).
\]
Together with \cref{wb:prop:workbench-holomorphic-form-vanishing} and Serre
duality \cite[\S13, Theorem~4, p.~22]{Serre1955Duality}, this fixes every
entry except the four middle entries, with
$h^{1,2}=h^{2,1}=m$ and $h^{1,1}=h^{2,2}$.

The verified integral sphere topology gives $c_1(X)=c_2(X)=0$ and
$\int_Xc_3(X)=2$.  In complex dimension three,
\begin{align*}
 \operatorname{td}(X)
 &=1+\frac12c_1+\frac1{12}(c_1^2+c_2)+\frac1{24}c_1c_2,\\
 \operatorname{ch}(\Omega_X^1)
 &=3-c_1+\frac12(c_1^2-2c_2)
   -\frac16(c_1^3-3c_1c_2+3c_3).
\end{align*}
Hirzebruch--Riemann--Roch for arbitrary compact complex manifolds
\cite[Theorem~3, p.~427]{AtiyahSinger1963} hence gives
\[
 \chi(\Omega_X^1)=-\frac12\int_Xc_3=-1.
\]
The already known zero entries reduce this identity to
$-h^{1,1}+h^{1,2}=-1$, proving $h^{1,1}=m+1$.
\end{proof}

This specializes the general constraints of Gray and Ugarte; a convenient
published synthesis is Angella \cite{Angella2018}, while the second-page
symmetry and inequalities originate in \cite{Ugarte2000}.  The argument
above uses the stronger candidate-specific direct images and form
vanishings, rather than assuming a general Hodge pattern for a hypothetical
complex $S^6$.

\subsubsection{the complete Fr\"olicher page}\label{inv:wbproof:thm:frolicher-e2-candidate}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:C1.1}.


\begin{proof}
Fr\"olicher's original construction identifies $E_1$ with Dolbeault
cohomology and $E_\infty$ with the associated graded de Rham cohomology
\cite[p.~643, Lemmas~1--2 and Theorem~3]{Frolicher1955}.  The table in
\cref{wb:thm:parametric-hodge-diamond} leaves only the displayed
$q=1$ and $q=2$ row complexes between the endpoint classes.  Since
$H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(X;\mathbb C)=0$ for $1\le k\le5$, every middle
$E_\infty^{p,q}$ is zero.  There is only one a priori possible higher
differential between middle positions,
$d_2:E_2^{0,2}\to E_2^{2,1}$, but already
$E_1^{0,2}=H^2(X,\mathcal O_X)=0$.  Every other $d_r$ with $r\ge2$ has
zero source or target by the same Hodge table.  Thus $E_2=E_\infty$, so the
two rows must be exact.  The ranks follow from their dimensions.
\end{proof}

The theorem explains why neither topology nor the Fr\"olicher sequence alone
can select a value of $m$: the two exact row complexes exist numerically for
every $m\ge0$.  The singular-fibre calculation below supplies the missing
analytic information.

\subsection{Generic maximal variation and its elliptic zero}

The most tempting shortcut to the remaining Hodge number is to treat the
Kodaira--Spencer matrix as invertible everywhere.  The following calculation
shows precisely what is true and what is false.

\subsubsection{determinant of the printed period derivative}\label{inv:wbproof:prop:period-derivative-determinant}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:A2.1}.
Write $K=6\dot\mu^{\,2}-\dot\tau\dot\beta$, where the dot differentiates on the marked upper half-plane.


\begin{proof}
At the cusp, \cref{wb:prop:period-input-audit} gives
\[
 t=e^{2\pi i s},\qquad Z=sB_0+C(t),\qquad
 B_0=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},
\]
with $C$ holomorphic at $t=0$.  Hence
\[
 \frac{dZ}{ds}=B_0+2\pi i\,tC'(t),
 \qquad
 \det\!\left(\frac{dZ}{ds}\right)=1+O(t).
\]
The cusp coordinate $s$ is locally biholomorphic on the marked cover, so
$K$ is nonzero near the punctured cusp and therefore is not identically
zero.

Now put $\rho=e^{\pi i/3}=\tau(z_1)$.  The difference between $\mu$ and
the local affine solution
\[
 \mu_1=\frac{2-\tau}{3}
\]
vanishes to order at least two at $z_1$: the homogeneous line has local
generator of order two there.  Since $\tau-\rho$ has a simple zero,
\[
 \dot\mu(z_1)=-\frac13\dot\tau(z_1).
\]
Write
\[
 \phi_1=2-\frac{6(1-\mu)^2}{\tau},
 \qquad \beta\circ g_1=\beta+\phi_1.
\]
Using $\rho^2-\rho+1=0$ and the preceding derivative gives
\[
 \dot\phi_1(z_1)
 =-\frac23(1+\rho)\dot\tau(z_1).
\]
The derivative of the linearized order-three action at its fixed point is
$g_1'(z_1)=-\rho$.  Differentiating the transformation law for $\beta$
therefore yields
\[
 -(1+\rho)\dot\beta(z_1)=\dot\phi_1(z_1),
 \qquad
 \dot\beta(z_1)=\frac23\dot\tau(z_1).
\]
Substitution gives
\[
 K(z_1)=6\left(-\frac13\dot\tau(z_1)\right)^2
 -\dot\tau(z_1)\left(\frac23\dot\tau(z_1)\right)=0.
\]
\end{proof}

The zero divisor of $K$ cannot be read from the single equality $K(z_1)=0$.
It is determined below only after the invariant lattices at the two multiple
fibres have been inserted.  This distinction is essential: direct image does
not commute with taking the dual lattice at a ramified coarse fibre.

\subsection{Logarithmic cotangent direct images}

Put
\[
 B=\mathbb P^1,\qquad
 \Sigma=p_0+p_1+p_2,\qquad
 D=f^{-1}(\Sigma)_{\mathrm{red}}=W+S_1+S_2,
\]
and set
\[
 \mathcal L=\Omega_B^1(\log\Sigma)\simeq\mathcal O_B(1),\qquad
 \mathcal A=\Omega_X^1(\log D),\qquad
 \mathcal E=\mathcal A/f^*\mathcal L.
\tag{WBH.11.1}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.1}
\]
At the cusp the local equations $t=z_1\cdots z_r$, $1\le r\le3$, show
directly that $\mathcal A$ and $\mathcal E$ are locally free.  At a finite
fibre the covering family has divisor $s=0$, the cyclic action is free on the
total space, and $dt/t=m\,ds/s$; hence its locally free logarithmic sequence
descends through the finite \`etale quotient.  Thus everywhere one has the
logarithmic conormal sequence
\[
 0\longrightarrow f^*\mathcal L\longrightarrow\mathcal A
 \longrightarrow\mathcal E\longrightarrow0.
\tag{WBH.11.2}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.2}
\]
The local $d\log$ bases and their relative form, including
$t=\prod z_i^{e_i}$ and analytic base change, are the logarithmic conormal
formalism of \cite[Chapter~II, \S3.2--3.3, pp.~72--75]{Deligne1970}; the
display above also follows directly from the stated local equations.

\subsubsection{the three logarithmic relative direct images}\label{inv:wbproof:prop:log-relative-direct-images}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:A1.2}.


\begin{proof}
At the cusp, the toric coordinates give
\[
 \mathcal E|_{N_0}
 =\mathcal O_{N_0}[d\log x_1]\oplus
  \mathcal O_{N_0}[d\log x_2].
\tag{WBH.11.3}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.3}
\]
Indeed a quotient shear changes each $d\log x_i$ only by a holomorphic
multiple of $d\log t$, which is zero in $\mathcal E$.  The already proved
structure-sheaf calculation therefore gives free local direct images of
ranks $2,4,2$ at $p_0$.

We now keep the ramification at $p_j$.  Write
\[
 A=\mathbb C\{t\},\qquad C=\mathbb C\{s\},\qquad t=s^m,
 \qquad (m,a)=(3,2)\text{ or }(4,1).
\]
Cartan's analytic quotient theorem identifies local holomorphic functions on
the quotient with invariants \cite[\S1, Theorem~1, pp.~1--2]{Cartan1954Quotient}.
The action on the total space is free, so the quotient map is finite \'etale;
the corresponding locally free sheaves and their equivariant structures
descend by finite \'etale descent.  This sheaf statement is not being
attributed to Cartan's theorem on invariant functions.  Finite pushforward
is exact, and Reynolds averaging
$v\mapsto |G_j|^{-1}\sum_{g\in G_j}gv$ makes the invariant functor exact in
characteristic zero.  Hence
\[
 R^qf_*\mathcal E|_{D_j}
 =\bigl(\pi_*R^q\widetilde f_*\widetilde{\mathcal E}\bigr)^{G_j}.
\tag{WBH.11.3a}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.3a}
\]
Choose equivariant frames $e_0,e_1$ of the relative cotangent and
$b_0,b_1$ of $R^1\widetilde f_*\mathcal O$ whose semilinear characters are
respectively
\[
 (1,\zeta^a),\qquad (1,\zeta^{-a});
\]
$b_0$ is the nowhere-zero class $\gamma^{0,1}$.  These may be chosen as
holomorphic constant-character frames, rather than merely as eigenvectors on
the central fibre.  Indeed, if $w$ lifts a $\nu$-eigenvector at $s=0$, then
\[
 P_\nu(w)=\frac1m\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\nu^{-k}(g^*)^kw
\]
satisfies $g^*P_\nu(w)=\nu P_\nu(w)$ and has the same nonzero central value;
after shrinking the disc, the projected eigenvectors form a frame.  On the
marked torus family the projection formula gives
\[
 R^q\widetilde f_*\widetilde{\mathcal E}
 \simeq
 (\mathcal O e_0\oplus\mathcal O e_1)
 \otimes
 \bigwedge^q(\mathcal O b_0\oplus\mathcal O b_1),
 \qquad 0\le q\le2.
\]
Solving
$\nu\zeta^r=1$ for the invariant exponent gives the following \emph{actual}
$A$-bases:
\begin{align*}
 f_*\mathcal E:\quad& e_0,\ s^{m-a}e_1,\\
 R^1f_*\mathcal E:\quad&
 e_0b_0,\ s^ae_0b_1,\ s^{m-a}e_1b_0,\ e_1b_1,\\
 R^2f_*\mathcal E:\quad&
 s^ae_0(b_0\wedge b_1),\ e_1(b_0\wedge b_1).
\tag{WBH.11.4}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.4}
\end{align*}
For comparison, the variable tangent lattice is generated by $s^av_1$.
Thus evaluation of the descended variable cotangent on the descended
variable tangent is $s^m=t$, not a unit.  This proves explicitly why
\[
 f_*\mathcal E\longrightarrow(f_*T_{X/B})^\vee
\]
is multiplication by $\operatorname{diag}(1,t)$ locally, although
$\mathcal E^\vee\simeq T_{X/B}$ before direct image.  This last identity is
an identity of locally free relative sheaves, not an assertion that formation
of the kernel commutes with taking a tangent-space fibre.  For example, at a
triple chart
\[
 R=\mathbb C\{x,y,z\},\qquad t=xyz,
\]
one has
\[
 T_{X/B}=\ker\!\left[R^3\xrightarrow{(yz,xz,xy)}R\right].
\]
If $yz\,u+xz\,v+xy\,w=0$, reduction modulo $x$ and $y$ gives
$u=xU$ and $v=yV$, and cancellation in the domain gives
$w=-z(U+V)$.  Hence
\[
 T_{X/B}
 =R(x\partial_x-z\partial_z)\oplus
  R(y\partial_y-z\partial_z)
 =\mathcal E^\vee.
\]
The kernel of the pointwise linear map $df_x$ at the triple point is
three-dimensional, whereas the fibre of this sheaf kernel is
two-dimensional: tensoring the kernel sequence with the residue field is
not left exact because the image ideal $(xy,xz,yz)$ is not flat.  Thus a
section can be nowhere zero in $T_{X/B}=\mathcal E^\vee$ even when its image
in the ambient tangent-space fibre vanishes.

The invariant vertical field $\xi$ gives a trivial subline of
$V:=f_*T_{X/B}$; the quotient has the reciprocal automorphy of the Hodge
line $\mathfrak K\simeq\mathcal O(1)$ from
\cref{wb:lem:hodge-line-audit}.  Since $H^1(\mathcal O(1))=0$, the resulting
extension splits:
\[
 V\simeq\mathcal O\xi\oplus\mathcal O(-1),
 \qquad V^\vee\simeq\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(1).
\]
Evaluation gives a generically invertible map
$f_*\mathcal E\to V^\vee$.  Formula \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.4} shows that its elementary
divisors are $(1,t)$ at each of $p_1,p_2$ and $(1,1)$ elsewhere.  Thus its
cokernel has total length two and
\(\deg(f_*\mathcal E)=1-2=-1\).  Evaluation on $\xi$ is stalkwise
surjective: the covector dual to the fixed eigenvector is a unit generator
at the cusp and in both finite invariant bases.  Its kernel is consequently
a line bundle of degree $-1$, and
\[
 0\longrightarrow\mathcal O(-1)\longrightarrow f_*\mathcal E
 \xrightarrow{\operatorname{ev}_\xi}\mathcal O\longrightarrow0.
\]
Because $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))=0$, this extension also splits, proving
\[
 f_*\mathcal E\simeq\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(-1).
\]
Also, by 
\cref{wb:thm:structure-direct-images-audit},
\[
 G:=R^1f_*\mathcal O_X=\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(-1),
 \qquad R^2f_*\mathcal O_X=\det G=\mathcal O(-1).
\tag{WBH.11.5}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.5}
\]
Here is the global filtration implicit in those bases.  Choose the
degree-zero summand in the preceding split sequence so that its generator
evaluates to one on $\xi$; locally this is the fixed eigen-covector $e_0$.
Together with the fixed class $b_0=\gamma^{0,1}$, take the corresponding
saturated sublines in $f_*\mathcal E$ and $G$.  Formula \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.3} at the cusp
and the bases \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.4} at the finite points show that these sublines are locally
generated by $e_0,b_0$ and that their quotients are locally generated by
$s^{m-a}e_1,s^ab_1$; hence both inclusions and both quotients are locally
free.  The evaluation splitting and Hodge-line calculation identify the two
filtrations as
\[
 0\subset\mathcal O\subset f_*\mathcal E,\qquad
 0\subset\mathcal O\subset G,\qquad
 \operatorname{gr}(f_*\mathcal E)=
 \operatorname{gr}(G)=\mathcal O\oplus\mathcal O(-1).
\]
Over the smooth locus the cup-product identification is
$R^1f_*\mathcal E=(f_*\mathcal E)\otimes G$.  Formula \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.4} extends its four
character lines as saturated rank-one subsheaves over all of $B$.  Three
associated-graded lines are generated locally by
$e_0b_0,s^ae_0b_1,s^{m-a}e_1b_0$ and have degrees $0,-1,-1$.  On the fourth,
the separately descended factors would
give
\[
 (s^{m-a}e_1)(s^ab_1)=t(e_1b_1),
\]
whereas $e_1b_1$ itself is invariant.  Thus that graded line is the upper
modification of $\mathcal O(-2)$ at $p_1+p_2$, hence is $\mathcal O$.
Similarly, the two graded lines of $R^2f_*\mathcal E$ are
$\mathcal O(-1)$ and
$\mathcal O(-2)(p_1+p_2)=\mathcal O$.  Every extension between the resulting
degree-zero and degree-minus-one lines splits: its $\operatorname{Ext}^1$
is one of $H^1(\mathcal O(-1))$, $H^1(\mathcal O)$, or
$H^1(\mathcal O(1))$, all zero.  This proves the three asserted splittings.
This is also the elementary filtered form of the
Birkhoff--Grothendieck classification
\cite[Theorem~2.1, p.~126]{Grothendieck1957}; the divisor modifications and
$\operatorname{Ext}^1$ identifications may equivalently be read in
\cite[Tags 0C6K, 0B3A, and 01XT]{StacksProject}.

Finally, \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.3a}--\eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.4} make every direct image free of ranks $2,4,2$ at
the finite points; \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.3} does the same at the cusp, and the smooth locus is
standard.  The multiple-fibre base change can also be read directly from the
invariant modules.  The Reynolds idempotent is $A$-linear, so invariants
commute with arbitrary finite $A$-base change.  For the scheme-theoretic
special fibre,
\[
 C\otimes_AA/(t)=C/(s^m),
 \qquad
 \bigl((C/(s^m))v\bigr)^G=\mathbb C\,s^rv
\]
on a character line whose invariant exponent satisfies $0\le r<m$.
Every basis vector in \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.4} therefore survives reduction modulo $t$, and
the special-fibre dimensions are exactly $2,4,2$.  No $R^q$ with $q>2$
occurs.  Descending induction in analytic cohomology and base change then
makes every base-change map an isomorphism, including for the nonreduced
finite fibres; precisely the same criterion, with citation, is recorded in
the proof of
\cref{wb:thm:structure-direct-images-audit}; see in particular
\cite[Chapter~III, \S3, Theorem~3.4 and Corollary~3.10]{BS76}.
\end{proof}

\subsubsection{the logarithmic Kodaira--Spencer divisor}\label{inv:wbproof:prop:log-ks-divisor}
The following working-edition argument proves the corresponding assertion of \cref{inv:A2.1}.


\begin{proof}
On the smooth locus, the connecting construction and its
exterior-product Leibniz rule are the Gauss--Manin/Kodaira--Spencer
formalism of
\cite[\S2, equations~(5)--(10), pp.~202--204]{KatzOda1968}.
Katz--Oda work with a smooth algebraic morphism; the citation is not being
used as a logarithmic analytic special-fibre theorem.  In the present family,
Deligne's local monomial calculation supplies the locally split logarithmic
sequence \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.2} \cite[Chapter~II, \S3.3]{Deligne1970}.  Taking a local
splitting and a \v Cech representative, the connecting cochain is the
difference of the two splittings.  Since exterior product of cochains obeys
\[
 \delta(\alpha\wedge\beta)
 =\delta\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}
   \alpha\wedge\delta\beta,
\]
the two displayed connecting maps extend across every logarithmic chart and
satisfy the same Leibniz rule.  Thus the singular-fibre formula below is a
direct calculation from \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.2}, not an extrapolation of the Katz--Oda
hypotheses.
The determinant is a section of
\[
 \det(\mathcal L\otimes G)\otimes\det(f_*\mathcal E)^{-1}
 =\mathcal L^{\otimes2}\otimes\det G
   \otimes\det(f_*\mathcal E)^{-1}
 \simeq\mathcal O(2)\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\otimes\mathcal O(1)
 \simeq\mathcal O(2).
\tag{WBH.11.8}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.8}
\]
At the cusp, $Z=sB_0+C(t)$ and $dZ/ds=B_0+O(t)$, so it is a unit.  At a
finite point use $\ell=dt/t=m\,ds/s$.  In invariant determinant frames
with no normalization imposed against the raw marked frames, direct
calculation gives
\[
 \det\kappa_0
 =\varepsilon(t)m^{-2}s^{m+2-2a}K(s),
 \qquad \varepsilon(0)\ne0.
\tag{WBH.11.9}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.9}
\]
Here $\varepsilon$ is the nowhere-zero invariant holomorphic unit recording the two
frame normalizations; compatible eigenframes may be normalized so that
$\varepsilon=1$.  The dot in $K$ means $d/ds$ in the chosen linearizing coordinate.
Replacing $s$ by another such coordinate changes only the unit, so every
divisor and order calculation below is coordinate-independent.
Equivariance gives
\[
 \operatorname{ord}_sK\equiv2a-2\pmod m.
\tag{WBH.11.10}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.10}
\]
At $(m,a)=(3,2)$, 
\cref{wb:prop:period-derivative-determinant} supplies $K(z_1)=0$; hence the
right side of \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.9} has coarse order at least one.  At $(m,a)=(4,1)$,
the prefactor is $s^4=t$, so the coarse order is again at least one.
The two forced zeros exhaust the degree in \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.8}.  They are therefore
simple, there are no others, and \cref{inv:A2.1} follows from \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.9}--\eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.10}.

For completeness, we derive the coarse matrices rather than only recording
their shape.  Let
\[
 D_{\mathrm{KS}}(s)=(d_{rs}(s))_{0\leq r,s\leq1}
\]
be the Kodaira--Spencer matrix on the marked cover after the common factor
$ds$ has been removed.  Since $t=s^m$ and
$ds=(s/m)\ell$, passage from the marked frames to the actual invariant
frames in \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.4} gives
\[
 A=\frac{s}{m}d_{00},\qquad
 B=\frac{s^{1-a}}m d_{01},\qquad
 C=\frac{s^{1-a}}m d_{10},\qquad
 D_0=\frac{s^{m+1-2a}}m d_{11}.
\tag{WBH.11.10a}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.10a}
\]
The character of each expression in \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.10a} is trivial, so each is a
holomorphic function of $t$.  In the bases
$(e_0,s^{m-a}e_1)$ and $(b_0,s^ab_1)$ one consequently has the exact matrix
\[
 [\kappa_0]=\begin{pmatrix}A&tB\\ C&D_0\end{pmatrix}.
\tag{WBH.11.10b}\label{inv:wb:eq:11.10b}
\]
Its determinant is \eqref{inv:wb:eq:11.9}.  Applying the exterior-product Leibniz rule to
the four ordered generators
\[
